We address Chebyshev polynomial factorization using the extended polynomial division by cos values, constructing minimal equations of cos expressions in terms of finite fields and deriving a minimal division matrix through random sampling, presenting it as a solution to a linear system whose coefficients are drawn from the general linear group over a specific field. Additionally, we explain a Chebyshev polynomial factorization algorithm based on this minimal division matrix and present various numerical results demonstrating its efficiency.

The growing necessity to stabilize frequency and prevent unwarranted injection of low-frequency signals into electrical grids has prompted the development of advanced transformers with built-in dampening functions for oscillations. This research builds on a previous study to further explore two-core Symmetrical Phase Angle Regulating (SPAR) transformers and their applications in grid stabilization. Unlike the initial concept, which employed an additional control signal, this improved implementation auto-regulates to prevent instability and does so without requiring external signals or memory. The proposed SPAR configuration and its control mechanism have been analyzed, and it was found that it doesn't conflict with existing protection systems. Specifically, this study assesses and validates the system's performance against high-level and low-level magnetic vector control protection criteria. It is observed that when properly categorized and controlled, the system's magnetic energy and temperature operate within safe parameters. The efficacy of the system is confirmed through numerical simulation on a 12 kW three-phase test bed, and it was found that the cycle-on time in the proposed topology has no significant impact on power loss and temperature, thereby ensuring a long-lasting and efficient operation of the SPAR transformer. The study further indicates that the system's current and temperature behavior is influenced by a first-order dynamic system, and this can be effectively controlled by adjusting the system's damping and set-point levels. Finally, this research outlines the parameters that need to be optimized for efficient and reliable performance of the SPAR transformer in various operating modes.

The next-generation wireless networks, particularly those in the mmWave range, heavily rely on the practical application of the hybrid precoding strategy to balance processing costs and network performance. This paper addresses the performance optimization problem of a multi-server multi-group broadcast system using mmWave with a hybrid precoding system as its core component. To achieve this optimization, we first develop a preliminary algorithm that iteratively applies zero-forcing precoding to individual subgroups and post-multiplies them using singular value projection. While this algorithm offers optimal performance for 1-RP (one radio frequency unit per node) systems, we incorporate additional ideas to enhance its performance in the more complex M-RP systems, resulting in a hybrid encoding approach that combines the characteristics of zero-forcing and regularized zero-forcing techniques. Furthermore, we propose a hybrid encoding performance improvement method that utilizes the concept of channel correlation. By leveraging these discoveries, we develop a hybrid encoding-based M-RP broadcasting strategy that yields superior performance, surpassing not only traditional M-RP systems, but also 1-RP systems equipped with more advanced precoding methods such as maximum-ratio combining.

A group is considered 'almost expander' if the average number of new elements produced when g^n is applied is close to 1, as n approaches infinity. In this study, it is demonstrated that finitely presented groups with high efficiency but near exponential growth rates, are indeed almost expander. The lower bound for the new elements produced when g is applied, is 99.9999% of the total, for any choice of g. This result is derived from a theorem which implies that densely embedded subgroups within a group of near exponential growth, maintain a similar property. The proof involves constructing a collection of nearly independent elements, leveraging the group's near exponential growth and a randomly generated matrix whose entries are drawn from the group. The formulated techniques can also be used to show that certain groups, such as surface groups and negatively pinched hyperbolic groups, possess densely embedded subgroups of similar growth rates.

We've determined the exponential stability of a certain star network composed of beams using a semi-group approach. In this system, every node except one is connected to a central node, forming a geometrically complex structure. Simplifying the model helps us assess the stability of the network by considering the diffusion processes along the branches to be identical. As a result, we've obtained an explicit exponential stability criterion for the network. This criterion relies on several key factors, including the lengths of the branches, their associated exponents, and the central node's internal processes. To validate our findings, we've performed a complementary numerical analysis.

For the purposes of investigating and understanding nucleosynthesis in extremely metal-poor stars and the source of heavy elements ($r$-process), accurate and precise nuclear mass values are essential. This is because these masses have a direct impact on the likelihood of beta decay. In our study, a advanced machine learning method, using accelerated neural network design, was able to predict nuclear masses with a high degree of precision using existing data on nuclear energy differences as training information. This model was able to accurately predict nuclear mass values to a high degree of precision even for previously unmeasured elements. In particular, it was able to predict one-keV precision for elements with atomic numbers greater than 82. This level of precision is necessary for investigating the $r$-process, as it allows for the accurate determination of nuclear mass values for elements that have not had their masses directly measured.

High-precision measurements of the dielectric material sapphire in the microwave frequency realm have been conducted at extremely low temperatures. By using this dielectric in the context of superconducting qubit measurements, our findings reveal the effects of thermal fluctuations on the dielectric, resulting in an at-the-wire (ATW) contribution with a mere change of $10^-$3. To arrive at this highly accurate measurement, a novel technique involving the simultaneous measurement of two closely-related qubits has been developed, yielding an impressive statistical variance reduction of $10^-$3 compared to individual qubit measurements. Furthermore, this research also showcases the effectiveness of this new measurement approach for an increasing number of qubits, presenting an alternative method for the study of dielectric interactions with the potential for widespread application.

The pull, a recently introduced concept, quantifies the deviation in the performance of a model relative to a baseline that achieves optimal results with perfect features. This concept has primarily been used in the context of image classification. This work takes a different approach, focusing on a different type of pull, specifically one based on optical (or radar) measurements that involve data such as scatter, brightness, or color. This is done for a simplified scenario in which a target's features are described solely by the reflectivity distribution. This distribution is modeled after the extent of the distribution based on the standard Rytov variance definition. This study calculates the Cram\'er-Rao limits for this distribution and defines the optimal sensor characteristics that maximize the target's information. Additionally, we examine the effect of finite aperture sizes on this information and compare it to existing sensors such as speckle radar or cameras. This work also defines a metric to evaluate the performance of scattering models and provides guidelines for utilizing this metric during model development.

This paper introduces an exact calculation method for Lagrangian relaxation dual values in two-stage robust optimization problems involving uncertain coefficients with binary ambiguity sets. For general linear optimization problems in the second stage, we derive a specific configuration to compute the dual value by solving a binary integer linear programming problem. We provide an exact formula for the Lagrangian dual value and prove its feasibility. This is exemplified in piecewise linear loss functions and network flow problems. Furthermore, we reformulate the original robust optimization problem using the Lagrangian relaxation dual objective function and develop a duality-based approach for approximately solving robust linear programming problems. This technique yields an optimal solution of the original problem and is at most a relative entropy deviation away from feasibility. This approximation is initially analyzed in the context of two specific problems: a multi-machine job scheduling and a multi-commodity flow optimization. Both problems are known to be NP-hard and we demonstrate that our approximation results in an optimal solution with improved quality compared to existing methods.

The study proposes the creation of a statistical dataset ('H4M') containing various types of data, including demographic, economic, transportation, air quality, and educational information, to study relationships between diverse factors in a comprehensive manner. This dataset is designed to analyze numerous phenomena, such as the impact of policies on air quality and transportation, as well as the correlation between economic factors and educational performance. To address these queries, we develop a multi-faceted approach that incorporates data from different sources, including administrative records, publicly accessible platforms, and educational databases. The 'H4M' dataset is unique in its holistic vision, offering a wealth of information to researchers and policymakers to explore relationships between diverse data sources and evidence-based decision-making. This dataset is available online at a specified repository URL.

The term Big Data encompasses various social, economic, and scientific phenomena, gathering significant attention from researchers and practitioners in recent years. This paper presents a cutting-edge visual data analysis framework centered around a user-friendly interface to systematically explore multidimensional data sets. Leveraging a combination of domain knowledge and statistical methods, the interface aids in data mining by generating insightful visualizations. Case studies utilizing social network interactions and financial transactions with high volumes and complexities demonstrate the efficacy of our innovative approach.

Recent advancements in graph neural networks have shown promising results in various applications. Yet, selecting the right neural architecture for a given problem task remains a significant challenge due to the vast array of existing models. In an effort to address this issue, the concept of transfer learning – previously successful in image-based learning – is being explored in the graph realm. The core idea revolves around identifying architectures that can serve as a shared starting point or adapt to specific problems, thereby enhancing performance. The study at hand seeks to establish transfer learning as a viable approach for graph neural learning architectures. The findings illustrate that transfer learning can yield improvements of up to 115.79% in test accuracy across six datasets, thereby validating its practical application in graph neural learning architectures. Moreover, the study shows that transfer learning can positively impact performance even when limited to architectures of reduced complexity. The associated code is available on GitHub at the indicated location.

The ultimate goal of artificial intelligence is to create self-sustaining systems that achieve their objectives through logical decision-making processes. A critical component in attaining this goal is the development of an intelligent suggestion system (ISS) capable of guiding system users toward the best possible choices to realize their goals. In this study, we introduce a decision-making model that incorporates dual feature allocation, which enables ISS to suggest specific values for user variables to aid goal attainment. The proposed method utilizes linear programming to determine the optimal variable values, and to enhance ISS usability, we incorporate two practical features: constraint checking to prevent illogical suggestions and consistency with user intent, and long-term decision-making to prioritize ISS recommendations that support ultimate goal achievement. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted to assess ISS performance, involving multiple case studies derived from various real-world problem sources. The issued Java Development Kit (JDK) source code facilitates ISS implementation, making the technology more accessible to the public.

The problem of determining if there's a single binary vector present within a family of $k$ vectors is crucial in many computational issues, specifically regarding set disjointness. Although this problem is known to be difficult to solve from a computational standpoint, under the assumption that partial sums can be computed efficiently (a common non-uniform model), a straightforward proof exists that demonstrates its resolution through a single pass in $O(k)$ space. Furthermore, this proof relies on little more than the assumption that any given vector contains at least one positive element within each subset. Subsequently, this method can also be applied to resolve the problem of $P$-property detection without relying on the assumption that counting queries can be performed. As a result, this approach offers a novel single-pass algorithm with $O(p + \log N)$ space for some specific types of problems, such as the $LC$-property and $Semiperfect$ property. Given the well-established difficulty in this specific problem, our method represents a non-standard solution.

Our study examines the spin stiffness within the paramagnetic phase of Heisenberg magnets, revealing a specific relationship between spin stiffness and momentum. The spin stiffness exhibits unusual momentum dependence and is not analytically representable in terms of the momentum throughout the paramagnetic phase. The critical exponents derived from spin stiffness show deviations from the theoretical values predicted by the Ginzburg-Landau theory, which assumes an analytically representable relationship. The discrepancy between the actual critical exponents and the predicted values increases in proportion to the fourth power of the momentum angle.

A single atom is captured and retained within an optical micro-trap by using an optical 3D lattice that directs it to the desired location. After capture, the atom is held in place by surrounding a smaller trap formed by multi- and inter-diffraction patterns. Additionally, a multi-diffraction grating is used in atomic alignment to create a detectable optical signal along the atom's axis. Our study presents an experimental method to produce these intricate patterns without the need for precise alignment, which is essential for the atomic alignment. This technique offers the potential to control the interaction between light and individual atoms as well as very low-energy protons, making it a foundation for developing atomic-scale photonic devices.

The behavior of the transverse electric field in a rotating two-dimensional system with a magnetic field can be understood through a general theoretical approach. This theory, based on two fundamental principles, first shows that a finite current is generated in response to a minor deviation from equilibrium and, secondly, that this transverse electric current follows a linear relationship with the magnetic field strength when in a completely equilibrium state. This relationship is similar to the Hall effect but is influenced by correlations within the system. Additionally, studies have revealed that as interactions within the system increase, so too does its transverse electric response to a magnetic field, displaying a proportional relationship. However, when considering disorders within the system, while the system's overall transverse electric response to a magnetic field remains linear in terms of the magnetic field strength, the transverse electric response to particle energy does, in fact, exhibit a nonlinear effect. This theoretical framework is capable of being extended to systems with multiple types of particles.

Our goal in this research was to expand on the application of a time-resolved method, called direct transcription, for solving time-varying optimization problems. Through theoretical analysis and practical examples, we demonstrated that direct transcription, which converts a time-dependent problem into a finite-dimensional optimization problem with a large number of variables and constraints, offers several benefits. These advantages include an improved solution strategy, increased problem awareness, better numerical methods, and enhanced result interpretation. To facilitate better understanding, we provided a step-by-step guide on implementing direct transcription to tackle time-dependent problems. Furthermore, we made available the accompanying Python code, which is accessible via a public repository at https://github.com/ZJU-OPT-UA/LBPO-DDT. Our method was tested on a complex real-world challenge, such as ensuring a dual-patient ventilation strategy during the COVID-19 pandemic, which involves providing individual oxygen supply in a shared setup. Through this example, we hoped to contribute valuable insights to the field of time-dependent optimization.

We define a rational function $f$ as bicritical if it meets specific criteria at each of its distinct fixed points, which in turn allows us to categorize $f$ into one of two platforms, either $p_5$ or $p_6$. Our research focuses on understanding the structure of the platform groups associated with these iterations. Specifically, for the $p_5$ platform, our findings confirm that the group of the generic element is a Demuskin group with a particular rank, while for the $p_6$ platform, our results show that the group of the generic element exhibits an infinite rank and is characterized by a unique property related to its transfer to the second rational function $g = f^2$. Additionally, our definitions also account for exceptional cases where $f$ and $g$ share a common point, which in turn yields an alternative platform $p_6^*$ in such scenarios.

Two-dimensional semiconducting devices and new Mo and W based products rely on the unique properties of semiconducting Mo and W dichalcogenides. Their electron transport properties are heavily influenced by their surface properties, particularly their work function, as it determines the barrier potential of electrons. By using state-of-the-art computational methods to analyze layered Mo and W dichalcogenides, a thorough investigation of their work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity across a wide range of thicknesss is established. The research identifies how the thickness affects the surface properties, allowing the work function to be predicted for free-standing sheets. The findings also suggest that a layer's surface energy is directly related to its work function. The calculated surface properties can inform designers of new 2D semiconducting devices about the optimal layer thickness and composition for their specific applications.

Artificial neural networks have achieved significant success in a wide range of supervised learning tasks due to their flexible nature. However, the specific architecture of ANNs, with their distinct neural layers, hides their fundamental ability to perform universal computation. By revealing this ability, we can establish a more unified understanding of supervised learning, regardless of the employed algorithmic method. In this context, we explore the concept of "change transmission" as a framework for modeling computation, with particular focus on the delta lens, a more detailed and formalized approach to understanding universal computation. Using the delta lens, we demonstrate that any computational process, including those that rely on feedback and self-reference, can be characterized by a sequence of state transformations, where each transformation depends on the previous state. Building on this insight, we define a set of "universal update operators" that can be used to derive any subsequent state, given an initial state and a description of the desired computational process. These three components - the state space, update operators, and description - form the basis of a universal learning algorithm, which we believe offers a traditional neural network training method, which we will denote as the delta lens training method (DLT). By expressing DLT in a distributed form (parallel DLT, or pDLT), we show that it resembles the iterative process typical in neural network training, where a forward pass simulates the evolution of the state and a backward pass adjusts the parameters of the operators to minimize errors, drawing on the principles of

We've established a new, uniform bound that ensures certain expressions based on $j$-derivative smooth functions can be approximated by periodized polynomials of the same degree at arbitrary small distance from a set called the sign-changing wrap-up curve. Specifically, the approximation holds with an arbitrarily small error, denoted as $\delta^{\infty}>0$, in a region near this curve. In a related finding, our results imply the existence of uniform, almost-periodic representations for functions classified as $s$-smooth in a specific mathematical context.

A crucial challenge in the study of rarefied gases is solving the Boltzmann equation efficiently. Recently introduced fast iterative methods for this equation hold great promise, particularly when modeled in a particular $L^2$ norm. Nonetheless, there's still uncertainty about how these methods perform in other important norms. We investigate this by examining the $L^1$ norm, where existing iterative schemes have significant limitations. We extend an existing proof from $L^2$ to demonstrate the convergence of certain iterative methods in $L^1$. Importantly, the number of required iterations to achieve a specified error in $L^1$ significantly exceeds that in $L^2$. This surprise reveals a critical limitation to the potential of these fast iterative methods. We also use this finding to develop an error estimate for models of fluid flow influenced by rarefied gases. Given the straightforward nature of the $L^1$ norm, combining it with existing strategies should enhance the practical performance of these methods.

The Horizon-10T collaboration reported an observation of multi-modal, strongly
interacting particle dark matter (DM) in an underwater detector, characterized by a
declining energy spectrum. We find groupings of DM events within the Horizon-10T dataset,
consisting of multiple, low-energy pulses of a specified pattern (either triple or quadruple),
occurring within a fraction of a millisecond. These events are suggested to be the result
of Axion Quark Nuggets (AQN) collapsing into their fundamental form, a process known as "global winding." The observed pattern of these events, including their energy, spatial, and temporal arrangements, is an indicator of AQN properties, yielding a specific projected cross-section range and a determined DM mass range.

Data from the CMS experiment at the LHC's 7 TeV proton-proton collisions in 2010 and 2011 were analyzed, leading to a joint analysis of Higgs-like particle assessments in the two-photon decay channel. Following a covariance matrix-based approach, an observed cross section of 6.1 fb was reported for this specific decay, which, after combining with combined Higgs-like particle searches, yielded a joint signal strength of 0.72 with a associated 1 sigma uncertainty of 0.28. Additionally, 95% confidence limits on the signal strength were calculated at 0.83 and 0.61 for Higgs boson masses of 125.15 GeV and 126.25 GeV, respectively.

Let $p$ be a prime. Within the context of weight $n+1$ Siegel modular forms over $\mathbb{C}$, we establish the transfer of a crucial criterion for $p$-divisibility by replacing the conventional Fourier-Jacobi forms with a more generalized 'Fourier elements', which encompasses both classical Siegel modular forms and their Siegel cusp forms. This criterion will serve as the foundation for analyzing the space of $p$-admissible Galois representations associated with Siegel modular forms.

In the realm of Topology, a connected component of mappings that induce equivalent roof systems for fibrations is termed a rigid fibration equivalence class. The equivalence classes are numerous, and they play a significant role in understanding topological properties, particularly for surfaces and higher-dimensional manifolds. This research delves into the unique characteristics of these classes in the context of surface fibrations. Specifically, it identifies and analyzes the distinct rigid fibration classes for torus fibrations, and explores their relationship with reduced graph coverings and the complexity of these graph structures, including their bond number. What's more, this study demonstrates a strategy for systematically generating a complete list of the equivalent fibrations within a particular class, utilizing a'sequence of reduction'. In addition to these findings, there are corresponding results for upper surfaces and some initial outcomes on the interconnection with reduced coverings of surfaces.

The theoretical framework for studying the statistical properties of a Pauli crystal in two dimensions is established, drawing inspiration from the theoretical model for the melting of classical crystals. By applying this model, researchers have determined that the heat capacity diverges at the critical temperature and that the enthalpy exhibits linear temperature dependence within the temperature range where the phase transition occurs. Additionally, the findings suggest that Pauli crystals in two dimensions undergo a second-order phase transition and that the ratios of successive volume changes to their respective critical values remain constant across different temperatures. Furthermore, the results imply that the temperature-dependent compressibility is zero above its critical value and experiences a natural logarithmic singularity below it. Lastly, the study shows that the temperature-dependent magnetic susceptibility follows a specific power law within the temperature range where the phase transition occurs and that the ratios of successive temperature values to their critical values exhibit constant values that depend on the magnetic field intensity.

Research in neural networks has seen rapid advancement, driven by research into complex systems. Due to their ability to model complex functions, neural networks are particularly suitable for problems requiring state estimation and prediction in control systems. They have found widespread use in areas like signal processing and chemometrics. These applications frequently involve complex problems characterized by data that varies over time. Such problems are often defined by dynamic matrices. In such cases, neural networks can be trained to learn and predict time-variant matrices. We will discuss these applications and explore a specific method called Zeroing Neural Networks, which we will use to demonstrate predicting solutions to matrix problems. We will also share relevant research papers and demonstrate some examples. Note that this tutorial focuses on theoretical aspects and practical examples of predicting solutions to matrix problems using ZNN.

Deep neural networks are remarkably effective at performing image classification, but their predictive capabilities are not as reliable when it comes to distinguishing between similar images, and they can even be misled by minor changes to the input. The inherent limitations of the pixels used in these images serve as a useful guideline for improving classification accuracy. In natural light conditions, pixels can either be on or off, and the resulting perception is a combination of the surrounding pixels' average values. In order to develop an even more effective and robust classification system, we propose a perceptive field consisting of a central node and surrounding nodes, where only two possible states - on or off - are available for each node. This new perceptive field can be utilized in various forms, such as in the form of a Gaussian pool. By replacing the traditional Gaussian pool with the proposed perceptive field, we achieved breakthroughs in image classification on multiple benchmarks, specifically CubicNet on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets. Moreover, our perceptive field led to significant enhancements in the robustness of the models by minimizing the impact of the input noise and adversarial attacks. The code for the proposed perceptive field and the adversarial attacks is available at: https://github.com/PerceptiveField/PerceptiveField.

We focus on advanced techniques for enhancing the capabilities of X-ray optics, specifically for broad-field applications. I'll provide an overview of these techniques, detailing how they work and the advantages they offer. It's essential to note that these methods either maintain or improve the spatial resolution of the optics while increasing their coverage area. I'll also discuss how each technique contributes to the future development of powerful X-ray observatories in space.

The core of topological insulators lies in their edge or surface states, which due to the lack of time reversal symmetry, become magnetically unstable. Introducing a magnetic field allows these states to become robust once more. A significant discovery has been made about the magnetic spectrum of twisted bilayer graphene under specific environmental conditions. Initially, it is discovered that a uniform global flux does not impede the occurrence of magnetic states with no nodal lines. Furthermore, an astonishing finding indicates the existence of states with flat energy levels near the Dirac points, which result from the combination of twisted and magnetic fluxes. Interestingly, these states transition into well-studied non-magnetic states under a particular configuration. The non-linear relationship between magnetic and twisted fluxes generates multiple stable states with various properties. The present research examines the theoretical foundation for these relationships and showcases the potential for controlling states with flat energy levels in twisted bilayer graphene under high magnetic flux environments.

Our proposed algorithm uses an LSTM architecture to suggest innocuous text based on a secret input, breaking down the input into its numerical vector representation, an operation that would normally be performed by the widely used Word2Vec algorithm. While maintaining the same computational simplicity as its non-encrypted counterpart, our algorithm significantly increases the difficulty of discovering its existence by evading detection using advanced statistical techniques, notably the random forest method. To validate its efficacy in generating plausible text, our algorithm was successfully tested in creating fake passages about Abraham Lincoln, and also applied the solution to an encrypted version of a problem in machine learning, specifically an encrypted multi-class classification task.

The energy sector's transition to decentralized power generation, such as solar and wind energy, necessitates an adjustment in how power systems operate. However, existing power systems are built upon assumptions made invalid by these changes, thus requiring corrections. Specifically, the standard power system model includes assumptions that are broken when decentralized generation is widespread, leading to substantial modeling errors. Notably, the assumptions surround power supply contracts and power export. This research develops a computational model to assess the impact of such errors during unit commitment planning. The model assembles combinations of power supply contracts and power export that are feasible from a practical standpoint and calculates the expenses associated with these combinations. The researchers have utilized the model to identify limitations in fast computation solutions for unit commitment planning problems. The study provides suggestions for power system operators to consider when evaluating combinations of power supply contracts and power export.

We conducted PWD experiments, XRD, and magnetic property measurements on polycrystalline, single-crystalline, and oriented samples of $\alpha$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$. The results reveal that the material undergoes dimerization under pressure, as indicated by a shift in the XRD peak at ~ 67.5 degrees related to an in-plane square lattice. This dimerization occurs at nearly the same pressure as the collapse of antiferromagnetic order visible in magnetic property measurements. We demonstrate that the material's magnetic properties correlate with lattice changes even after the material's structural transformation has occurred. Notably, the electronic gap, undetectable in our experiments below a 7 GPa, increases with pressure in conjunction with these lattice changes. These findings provide essential insights for understanding Kitaev materials, especially in relation to quantum spin liquid behavior.

The synthetic control method has become a widely recognized approach for evaluating the effect of treatment on a specific unit, such as a local government or a firm, by comparing it to a control group composed of similar units. This treatment effect can be determined in a variety of ways, such as through parallel covariates, propensity score matching, and interventions. Our research, however, takes a different route, centered on the idea that the control units' observations are merely approximations or simulations of the treated unit's outcomes, leading to the development of a new inference technique. This novel method can incorporate data-driven weights to improve accuracy, in contrast to traditional approaches. Our theoretical analysis supports the efficacy of this technique across diverse scenarios. Moreover, through a simulation study, we demonstrate that the traditional methods can sometimes produce less precise estimates compared to the proposed weights. Ultimately, we apply our framework to re-examine a renowned study, analyzing the impact of casino legalization in Kansas on its casino's financial performance.

Complex network structures can be found across numerous sciences, ranging from biological systems to social groups. The growing need for data analysis tools to understand and work with these complex networks has led to advancements in various fields. One particular tool, Gromov-Wasserstein divergence, enables researchers to compare and analyze the topological features of networks despite differences in dimension and scale. However, when applying this tool to multiple datasets, it's necessary to combine the structures while preserving the confidential information of the data sources, which presents a security risk. To address this concern, we have developed a method that uses local differential privacy to calculate the private Gromov-Wasserstein divergence locally on each dataset, allowing it to be shared anonymously. Subsequently, we combine the shared private divergences using a novel framework, which in turn facilitates the calculation of a unified structural metric for the combined networks. This metric, known as the Gromov-Wasserstein proxy, captures the combined network's structural characteristics without compromising confidential information. To validate the proposed method's effectiveness, we have conducted experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its ability to provide similar results to the original method using publicly accessible frameworks but with enhanced security. The method, described in this paper and implemented in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ucasJQ/sw-privacy-gromov, offers an important contribution to the field of structure-based network analysis.

The non-linear interaction between a high-intensity laser and plasma, containing a small amount of ions that can be oriented in different polarization states, has been investigated theoretically. This has led to an explanation for how the polarization state of the laser affects the formation of a plasma bubble. Specifically, it was found that a circularly polarized laser generates more efficiently than a linearly polarized one, leading to a greater electron population in the bubble. The theoretical results also predict the existence of a unique, self-regulating mechanism that adjusts the electron population according to the laser's polarization state, resulting in distinct acceleration patterns depending on the polarization state.

A platinum foil with a mass of 25 milligrams was studied over 200,000 hours of exposure as part of a search for unusual nuclear changes and signs of dark matter interactions. During the experiment, various types of decay and potential dark matter interactions were closely examined. The investigation found a maximum deviation from expected results in the range of $2 \times 10^{13}$ to $4 \times 10^{17}$ years for certain types of decay and $1 \times 10^{15}$ to $3 \times 10^{18}$ years for other types. The results also established new limits for certain types of nuclear changes and dark matter interactions, with particular emphasis on the $2\nu$ process. The findings further resulted in improved half-life estimates for several types of decay and served as a test for certain theories beyond the standard model of physics, with researchers hoping the results will contribute to further understanding of nuclear physics and the search for exotic interactions.

The calculation of the renormalization constants for the flavor-singlet axial-vector current operators is presented, along with the corresponding charge and its anomaly in a dimensional regularization scheme.

A crucial component of creating authentic, real-world imagery is texture and reflectivity. Current generative models fall short in producing realistic effects, especially when it comes to subtle color gradients, especially in scenarios involving multiple reflections and exposure variations. This research addresses this challenge by leveraging simultaneous observations from a pair of cameras capturing different light frequencies at varying intensities. A neural network is designed to generate a tinted image sequence that synchronizes and blends reflections and exposure variations, thereby enabling the creation of realistic global texture and color gradients in an end-to-end process. This approach is demonstrated through its successful capture of natural scenes with a dual-camera setup in multiple experimental environments, including vineyards, flowers, seaweed, and metal objects undergoing reflection and exposure variations. Our method is capable of producing undisturbed subjects while accurately replicating the effects of natural light and texture in an all-in-one process that eliminates the need for pre- and post-processing techniques.

A comprehensive investigation is conducted on the generalized $n$-dimensional Ermakov system. Specifically, we derive its Darboux vectors and determine the conditions under which the system's symplectic structure remains constant. Additionally, we explore the relationship between this system and the Nijenhuis Saito-Wu system.

We're focusing on the Inaccessible Transit Feed Specification (iTSFS), which blocks access to bus feed information as a security measure. To counter this, we've developed an approach using Deep Learning based Automatic Speech Recognition to convert spoken bus feed information into text, leveraging the existing microphone and ITFS-enabled bus for input. By combining the speech input with data-driven bus feed parsing, we can extract and display meaningful feed information from ITFS. The feasibility of our approach was tested through user trials, demonstrating positive results. Not only does our method overcome the accessibility barrier, but it also offers significant operational benefits for transportation systems.

Building upon the insight that similar objects share common characteristics, this research presents an innovative approach called Proto-Differentiation (PD) for classifying scarce data. By breaking down classes into distinct prototypes, each exhibiting unique characteristics, PD aims to amplify classification signals. Notably, PD surpasses methods focusing solely on individual samples or means, by learning representative prototypes that accurately characterize each class. Notably, PD's mathematical derivations yield well-defined loss and inference functions, facilitating efficient learning. In experiments, PD has demonstrated superior performance across various scenarios, including low-data settings, by outperforming state-of-the-art methods, as evidenced by our study's website: https://maenhautw.github.io/Proto-Differentiation/

We're analyzing systems with consistent yet temporarily unconfined symmetries, where time is used differently than in normal evolution. Our model includes a key assumption that a corresponding local score operator has a constant spectrum, a condition often met in theories where a global symmetry leads to the emergence of a similar local one. This assumption is connected to a'semi-dynamical' property where the average change in a system's properties over time is balanced by a corresponding change in its conjugate momentum. Developing this assumption to its fullest, we derive a comprehensive statement relating currents and associated external influences, ultimately broadening a longstanding statement about time-invariant symmetries. Our new result addresses its 'non-continuous' counterparts, discussing various characteristics in more general terms. This work also resolves a puzzle in the statistics of non-reversible symmetries, specifically by proving a deep connection between the concept of 'average action' and symmetry properties.

In a graph, G a semi-strong substructure is formed from edges (R) and irreducible edges are contained within it. A graph is semi-strong when every cycle using at least two directions can be closed using the direction of the edge in that cycle. When the graph is split, it contains a complete subgraph and an independent set, and in the context of semi-strong substructures, semi-strong cycles are of particular interest. It has been demonstrated that in split graphs, the maximum length of cycles in the graph is equal to the p value of the graph if and only if the maximum p value of the graph's weak supergraphs is equal to the p value of the graph, and this allows the confirmation of the graph's semi-strong SBC conjecture.

A cutting-edge approach for identifying tau particle decays in the CMS detector has been developed, leveraging a deep neural network. Hadronic decay patterns, consisting of three charged particles, are particularly challenging due to their similarity in shape and momentum to other background objects such as jets. The new technique utilizes a deep neural network with six layers to distinguish real tau decays from fake ones, with results showing an impressive improvement in performance over previous techniques by at least one order of magnitude. The accuracy in identifying genuine tau particles while rejecting fake ones exceeds 0.9 across a wide range of pseudorapidity values and average transverse momenta for taus above 1 GeV. The new software has been successfully incorporated into the CMS computing systems and is currently in use for analyzing real data from proton-proton collisions recorded during 2017.

Upcoming studies such as LSST and Roman are expected to send large amounts of data to scientists for analysis, requiring rapid categorization of diverse objects without prior knowledge. Traditional machine learning techniques, typically based on maximum likelihood estimation, may not effectively utilize all available information, particularly if the data is imperfect or the classes have uneven probabilities. We investigate the use of Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), which incorporate uncertainty in post-processing, as a superior method for such tasks. BNNs have the advantage of providing both predictions and uncertainty levels, allowing for improved performance in high-volume observations. We demonstrate the BNN approach through two case studies: the classification of galaxy and non-galaxy images, and the distinction between Type Ia and ordinary Type II supernovae events. We found that the BNN method surpasses a traditional machine learning approach in these areas, with a higher accuracy and lower uncertainty rate for galaxy classification and a greater than 90% accuracy in identifying Type Ia supernovae at a false positive rate of less than 1%. These results validate the BNN technique as a reliable and efficient tool for analyzing observations, with the method itself being easily modulated to accommodate various observation goals and resulting uncertainties.

Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering in
photonic crystal fiber, utilizing its spatial mode structure for analysis. By
launching a pump signal into a fundamental mode and monitoring the resulting
stimulated Stokes mode, we identify and accurately model a set of mode-
dependent efficient interactions with the fundamental zero order mode.
Building upon this understanding, we successfully induce intermodal Brillouin
scattering by launching multiple excited modes, achieving a significant rise in
Brillouin gain. For the first time, we demonstrate a hybrid scheme that combines
the benefits of single-mode and multi-mode Brillouin scattering, offering the
lower loss and higher on-off ratios associated with single-mode schemes while
frequently encountering the higher backscatter IDs and corresponding longer
confinement times characteristic of multi-mode scattering.

The Coxeter group foundation theorem has significant applications, particularly in Chevalley's theorem on group cohomology. For finite Coxeter groups, it was found that the theorem's proof relies heavily on combinatorial techniques, specifically tree pairs and the biased tree pair foundation theorem. Considering that biased tree pairs can be seen as a product of tree pairs and a group's generating set, one might anticipate that the theorem would hold for infinite Coxeter groups as well. For the $B_n$ type case, it was discovered that the theorem indeed holds under certain conditions regarding the group's generators. Furthermore, it was found that when the generators include all simple generators, the $B_n$ type group's $K$-group can be expressed in terms of a $G$-group $K$, where $G$ represents the group generated by these simple generators. In particular, this led to the discovery of a relationship between the $K$-groups of the alternating group and a quadratic group derived from the generators' Baues' $E_2$-algebra.

Two new problems, Set-Union Knapsack and Budgetized Coverage, emerge as vital tools in managing hybrid multi-objective optimization techniques, where the former allows covering things with given weights and the latter incorporates a budget constraint. These two problems are essentially equivalent and share a common solution space. We've effectively addressed these problems using an innovative local search method, which combines two unique operators, addition and removal, implemented on a graph-based representation of solutions. Our approach is exceptional for its capacity to avoid infeasibility using a specialized balancing method. Through various experiments on synthetic and real-world data, we demonstrate the superiority of our algorithm over alternative methods, including a simple local search and a more intensive genetic algorithm solution.

In online gambling, many players tend to stop playing within a short period of time. This common issue affects nearly every gaming business and is referred to as customer attrition. Identifying which players are likely to leave their platform is crucial for gaming companies to provide an attractive and engaging experience. Past methods relied on external data such as a player's past behavior, while a model was proposed in this study to predict a player's future actions based on real-time feedback. Integrating real-time feedback with a decision tree-based model significantly improved the accuracy of predictions in this context. When tested using data from a real-world online betting environment, the integrated model performed significantly better than traditional approaches and was able to accurately forecast which players are about to abandon the platform. Results showed a 23.9% improvement in accuracy compared to using historical data alone. Further analysis of the model's results revealed interesting insights into the types of customers who are at risk of abandoning the platform, including those who engage in high-risk behavior and those who do not feel connected to the community on the platform.

We have investigated the finite-temperature properties of the 2D scalar Ising field theory, particularly in the presence of a magnetic field, through the use of finite-temperature CFT at the microscopic level. This investigation utilized the underlying lattice theory, whose behavior can be described by a dual conformal field theory at both zero and finite temperatures. Our analysis at finite temperatures was facilitated by the incorporation of a real magnetic field, which enabled us to derive both the low- and high-temperature regimes of the magnetic susceptibility's dispersion relation. Our results accurately predict the magnetic field's effect on the number of degenerate CFT primary states at both zero and finite temperatures, particularly the influence of the Yang-Lee discontinuity at the critical point. Our method combines the lattice theory with conformal symmetry and holonomy symmetry, the latter being a finite-temperature manifestation of spatial parity.

We have established relationships between two key aspects of a theory that describes how quarks and gluons interact transversely: the gluon 'TMD' distribution and a calculation method called 'TMD-PDF', which relates to the quark 'TMD' distribution. Using this connection, we have demonstrated how to derive 'TMD-PDF' from a theory that describes the behavior of strongly-interacting particles, even in their ground state. Additionally, we have developed a method to compute the 'TMD-PDF' without relying on approximations or simulations involving effective interactions. Instead, we have developed a way to directly compute 'TMD-PDF' based on their underlying field-theoretic definitions. This method allows us to compute 'TMD-PDF' at any desired precision, including corrections that are proportional to a large number. Furthermore, we have identified an important region of momentum space, known as the 'PDF region', in which 'TMD-PDF' can be related to a type of function called a 'PDF'. Our relation between 'TMD-PDF' and this PDF allows us to make precise connections to experimental data and theoretical calculations involving strongly-intermittent phenomena related to gluons.

In the context of ultra-relativistic nuclear collisions, the interaction between light, low-momentum electrons and positrons and dense nuclei at various charges can be mathematically modeled. An explicit equation is derived for the continuous electron and positron production across a wide range of energies, taking into account the influence of nuclear form factors. Additionally, associated polar and longitudinal photon production is also considered in this analysis. Given that ultra-peripheral collisions primarily involve photon-nucleon interactions, the initial electron and positron spectra exhibit dependence on the photon nucleon cross section, as well as the appropriate flux factor involving nuclear form factors. An important consequence of the strong exchange of photons between the nucleons is the observed suppression of the electron and positron production due to the exclusion principle at energies near the nucleon mass. An exception to this suppression is observed at very low electron energies where the constraints imposed by the flux factor and the photon nucleon cross section lead to enhanced production. Calculations of the associated polar and longitudinal photon production also reveal other interesting phenomena such as the variation in yield ratios as a function of electron energy. These ratios are particularly significant at very low electron energies where the influence of the strong Coulomb field is diminished. These ratios are observed to be constant in a specific energy range. An attempt has also been made to gauge the feasibility of detecting these electrons and positrons in future experiments.

To enhance cyclist safety through intelligent mobility systems, reliable accident prediction models are crucial. However, existing research has been hampered by limited data, inadequate contextual factors, and the subjectivity of human-labeled data. The primary challenge lies in collecting and leveraging video-based data, accompanied by cyclist motion information. A groundbreaking approach has been developed that innovatively applies deep learning techniques to predict cyclists' motion patterns and assess risk levels. The risk estimator utilizes context-sensitive data regression to generate a continuous risk score along with x and y displacement predictions. Specifically, this model capitalizes on self-supervised sequence-to-sequence techniques, utilizing a pre-trained encoder-decoder model, to create a novel action-conditioned motion model. The continuous cyclistic stream of vehicle data allows for pre-training the model without labels from diverse traffic scenarios. Finally, a multi-task architecture is employed to incorporate risk prediction, using cyclist acceleration and turning angles as contextual factors to produce a more accurate risk score. The model demonstrates exceptional predictive skills on a newly-introduced dataset for cyclistic risk assessment, surpassing benchmarks for x and y displacement predictions. The successful implementation of this approach marks a significant step in using raw video data to predict cyclistic trajectories and quantify risk in real-time.

This research proposes a resilient robotic motion planning approach that achieves high-level objectives while minimizing the risk of collisions and critical system failures. The framework uses the principles of Control Barrier Functions to ensure safe and adaptive planning, even in dynamic and uncertain environments. The algorithm sets theoretical boundaries for stability and sets points of interest to maintain direction towards the goal. The evaluation demonstrates that this method can successfully navigate through complex spaces and maintain system stability with reduced error rates. The approach is successfully tested on a quadrotor drone in simulated environments with varying conditions.

For any ring R, we define the boundary numbers bound(R) as the minimum and maximum amounts respectively of n elements in R that divide all other elements in R, when considering univariate divisions. In contrast, we define the boundary numbers bound_R(n) as the minimum and maximum amounts respectively of n elements in R that divide all other elements in R, when considering multivariate divisions. These boundary numbers are explored in relation to various properties and subgroups of rings, particularly in relation to nilpotent and graded rings, where it is demonstrated that bound(R) is equal to the maximum nilpotency degree of subgroups in R and bound_R(n) has a lower bound that asymptotically equals n^1/(log n). However, it's also shown that bound(R) can be asymptotically equal to n, as well as bound_R(n) can be asymptotically equal to n, by using an example of a specific division in a quotient of polynomial rings. Furthermore, it's proven that bound(R) is equal to n, when considering a free algebra over a countable field divided by its ideal and divided by a parameter in that ideal.

Deep neural networks' (DNNs) inherent ability to generalize is considered one of the greatest breakthroughs of the past century. In order for DNNs to be utilized in high-stakes applications such as self-driving cars, their ability to generalize in unpredictable situations is essential, especially when contingent upon rare data. The ability of DNNs to handle instances that challenge their training is referred to as "robustness." Unfortunately, our current understanding of DNNs is hampered by instances that challenge their generalization, specifically those that cause them to misidentify critical information in unexpected conditions. The organic generalization strategy, developed in the paper "Towards Intrinsic Robustness of Deep Neural Networks", advocates for incorporating intrinsic robustness in DNNs. The underlying thesis is that an accurate organic generalization should hold unabated across various instances. By removing train-set biased assumptions from the organic generalization concept, this perspective could potentially extend its scope to encompass instances not yet seen during training, thereby making good generalization outcomes more dependable. In this paper, we aim to achieve this by proposing a novel organic generalization notion termed "Organic Robustness", which holds unreservedly across known and unknown instances alike. Additionally, we employ a "Know-your-Adversary" (KYA) strategy to identify and study the unknown instances that challenge DNNs' generalization, with a focus on enhancing their performance in unpredictable conditions. This study explores a broad category of non-reversible non-local transport models, where the flux is defined by an arbitrary function linking density and local velocity derivatives. Assuming a particular form of this function yields a non-intuitive non-local Euler equations with diverse characteristics beyond traditional hyperbolic models. A comprehensive examination is conducted to determine well-posedness and entropy admissibility in this expanded framework, with the use of an auxiliary variable to establish these properties. It is further demonstrated that the solutions to these expanded equations converge to the classical solution of a similar reversible model in the long term.

A dilation surface is an embedded surface in the extended plane that has a non-trivial action under the dilation group. This action creates a partition on the surface, dividing it into connected regions, and determining whether these regions are invariant or not has an important connection to the surface's topology. By expressing the dilation group's action as a vector field, which extends to the surface, we can use this to determine the partition's stability. This stability is directly linked to the surface's surfaces being at a steady point, and two specific areas on the surface split the dilation into its base forms. This partition's stability, in turn, is connected to the surface's topology. To understand how changes in the dilation occur, we can use a new type of connection in the dilation's flow graph, which describes the different ways the dilation can change. This change in the dilation's graph defines its dynamic behavior, which can either be in equilibrium or not. To understand the different states of the dilation's motion, we can use two different types of maps, which describe how changes in the transmission map occur. Either the transmission map either increases, decreases, or remains constant, which in turn indicates if the surface is changing, remaining the same, or shrinking. This behavior is understood through two separate types of maps which describe changes in the base, which are either increasing, decreasing, or remaining constant. The study of total association in cognitive processes has been overlooked, despite its potential to enhance our understanding of brain function. To address this gap, a novel metric for measuring the functional relationship between brain regions has been developed and used to create a total association network for the entire Cerebellum. Analysis of spatial and temporal characteristics of this network, along with correlation to existing functional connectivity data, reveal a new aspect of brain function. Moreover, its modularity and community structure were explored in detail. Building on this network, a multi-scale connectivity framework has been designed to investigate the functional relationship between large brain systems. Specifically, regional and long-distance connections within the total association network were examined to identify targets for further research. Finally, a conceptual framework for representing the functional connection of the whole human brain, known as the functional connectome, has been developed to integrate regional and long-distance connectivity metrics.

The classical Segal-Bargmann transformation, combining analysis and combinatorics, faces a significant obstacle in the context of spinors, where the non-commutative nature of the algebra h+ impedes a direct translation of its properties. However, within the framework of Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transform, the argument can be reinterpreted in a more fundamental way, revealing that the initial Segal-Bargmann transform is specifically tailored to accommodate zero-spin states. The limiting case of this spin-generalized transform is examined, yielding an equivalent representation of the space of square-integrable functions on spinor space as a subspace within the space of square-integrable Clifford algebra-valued functions on phase space. The resulting isomorphism restores the original structure of the space, combining analysis and combinatorics, while also demonstrating the irreversibility of the transformation. Building upon the Clifford algebra-valued Segal-Bargmann transform, a differential operator is constructed that acts as a universal Hamiltonian for all spin states within the space, thus effectively consolidating the collection of individual spin Hamiltonians into a single, more comprehensive operator.

In the context of a Gaussian field, we develop and justify a conditionally normal representation, where the field's values are reassigned based on their values in a smaller subset of the space, in an order that varies with the field's correlation coefficients. This representation has practical implications for approximating Gaussian fields at reduced computational cost, taking into account only a subset of the space's points that contribute most to the field's variability. Our method applies a field of covariance matrices on a nested sequence of increasing subspaces, where each addition of a new covariance matrix transforms the field's conditionally normal representation by adding a new 'layer' of variables. To efficiently compute the field's values in each iteration, we leverage properties of sparse matrices and eigenvalue decompositions. Additionally, we establish a criterion for selecting the optimal number of involved subspaces and demonstrate its applicability on a few exemplary fields, such as the class of fields with autoregressive properties and the Poisson-Lognormal integral, in conjunction with an efficient 'layered' approximation method for the field's probability distribution.

This study explores the potential for creating a robust and sprawling sensor network that leverages the sky as a key component. By designing a novel sensor node that utilizes dual antennas with distinct orientations, the collection of relevant wireless signals is enabled, facilitating the estimation of the node's location through channel analysis. By avoiding the incorporation of additional satellite devices or costly equipment like GPS, the integration of celestial signals into wireless communication systems presents an innovative approach. Though challenging, the use of signal strength for location estimation can be addressed with the development of efficient algorithms. In this context, a ground-and-sky sensor network refers to a system where some nodes have access to sky signals, while others do not. This work develops the concepts and locations estimation algorithms for such scenarios, demonstrating their effectiveness through simulation. Moreover, a prototype of the node is constructed, marking the initial culmination of this research, which aims to establish a full-scale, reliable network spanning the globe by harnessing the potential of celestial signals.

The successful resolution of several key issues has enabled the completion of the first fully-fledged generation of long-distance neutrino experiments based on large enhanced detectors, specifically the first complete stage of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). These developments, successfully implementing cutting-edge enhanced plastic scintillator technology on a large scale, have accurately assessed and refined their technical and operational processes. Consequently, DUNE is now ready to execute its comprehensive 6-year research program, commencing data collection in 2027. This study evaluates the current status of the DUNE project and its future prospects, emphasizing its comprehensive plan and the resulting scientific outcomes, and highlighting technical advancements and the modernization of industrial processes enabled by its initiatives.

A new technique for top identification in experiments has been created and optimized. The process, referred to as top tagging, assigns probabilities to subgroups of jets originating from the top quark based on their combination. The original algorithm used a decision tree to assign these probabilities, but improvements were made through new methods such as scanning, enhanced top tagging (ETT), and Monte Carlo (MC) training. ETT was developed as a hybrid of these methods and utilized a tree-based model with preselected variables. Testing on a dataset indicated that this method successfully tagged top quarks 65% of the time while misidentifying light quarks 5% of the time. The method was then analyzed using a new technique that breaks down the contribution of variables to the model's output. The result revealed that the most influential variable group in top tagging consists of the leading jet and the second highest transverse momentum of the top candidate, which accounted for 43% of the model's explanation.

This document establishes a foundation for the formalization of advanced Virtual Organization concepts related to their structure, functionality, and evolution, building upon previously defined basic components. It details the initial model and its components, addressing two key aspects: the initial structure of Virtual Organizations and their management through control actions. The formalization is realized using the Z Notation.

To accelerate the achievement of optimal policy solutions in reinforcement learning, particularly model-free reinforcement learning, we introduce a novel technique, variance-reduction-based experience replay (VR-ER). This approach leverages the similarities between successive states in the replay buffer to significantly reduce the variance of value estimates, thus enabling larger learning rate staircases and decreasing the required number of samples for convergence. Our theoretical analysis reveals that VR-ER achieves a substantial acceleration in the convergence rate, and numerical experiments demonstrate its benefits in various environments, leading to superior performance compared to traditional methods. The code supporting our findings is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zeyohung/vari ance-decrease-ER.

Two new methods, the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and superbosonization, have recently been proposed to address the "3-2-1" problem in the study of $U(N)$ invariant integrals in matrix models. Both techniques yield the same result for first-order path integrals and can be considered equivalent. However, at second-order, these methods differ in implementation and lead to the superbosonization equation, a specific formulation that leads to the most straightforward results. This difference in approach is explored further, with an emphasis on the more straightforward application of the superbosonization equation.

Recent studies in spatiotemporal predictive learning have achieved notable success in modeling dynamic weather patterns. Despite this progress, using encoder architectures based on ConvLSTM to extract detailed motion information is not optimal, as it incurs high computational costs. Furthermore, these traditional encoders only focus on the temporal dependencies of features generated by CNNs, neglecting the exploration of motion details within neighboring frames. To address this limitation, we present an efficient and generalized encoder architecture called MoDeRNN, which distills the information from adjacent frames and provides more detailed motion features. This architecture can be utilized as a flexible framework by integrating various CNNs to adapt to diverse applications. We validate the efficacy of MoDeRNN in handling precipitation and ocean current prediction, achieving a significant improvement in prediction accuracy while decreasing computational costs by 52% with similar model complexity.

This research aims to bridge the gap between programming languages used for systems development and those for general software development by adapting advanced type theories into a practical, general-purpose language. An existing prototype called Josephine has been built, implementing a substantial type system centered around the concept of effect types, along with a comprehensive suite of programming language features. Initially developed as part of the ERC grant on language development, this project involves a unique collaboration between a active general-purpose programming language development team and a research team focusing on advanced type theories. Through a co-design process, this project has incorporated insights from both theoretical and practical sources. An early prototype of the language has been created using the Rust programming language and its compiler, providing a functional platform for experimentation and safety evaluations. Focusing on runtime effect handling and effects with explicit start and end points, this project has devised a type system that naturally incorporates effects and provides syntax-based support for effect manipulation. An effects-based approach to handling errors in Josephine serves as a distinct alternative to error type approaches and has been informed by discussions around effect types and partiality in programming languages. An effects perspective on null references, for example, highlights the value of addressing the issue at runtime as opposed to solely addressing its static aspects. Building upon existing work in language design, this project has explored novel methods for collaborating effects and effect handling mechanisms, providing a substantial contribution to the field. An early implementation of the language using Rust and its associated challenges has also contributed to the project, showcasing the potential applications

The investigation of neutrinoless double-beta decay serves as a unique method for verifying the Majorana nature of neutrinos. However, the accuracy of experiments is limited by a significant source of background that arises from the same process but with neutrinos, and this issue persists throughout the entire range of neutrino masses that need to be tested. This particular type of decay is uniquely advantageous in certain laboratory settings with high-intensity neutrino beams. In such contexts, the creation of pairs of massive states with equal properties, known as Majorana states, can serve as a significant source of decay products at colliders. In this research, the study of neutrinoless double-beta decay in experiments involving high-intensity neutrino beams is explored, with a specific focus on a crucial phase change that occurs due to interactions between Majorana states.
