The results indicate that with the entire type-X 2HDM parameter space considered, it is capable of delivering a $2-6\sigma$ agreement with both the W boson mass and $(g-2)_\mu$ observations. Specifically, our analysis found that for the entire type-X 2HDM parameter space with $\tan\beta$ between 1 and 50 and with various values of $\lambda_3$, it is capable of delivering a $2-6\sigma$ agreement with both the W boson mass and $(g-2)_\mu$ observations.

Our proposed framework, SWIFTER, is designed to identify complex concepts within text data by leveraging crowdsourced input to create a set of specialized search queries. By using the responses to these queries, SWIFTER isolates concepts present in each answer and, based on user input, generates new queries to explore related concepts. Through a iterative process, SWIFTER continuously refines its concept detection capabilities by expanding its concept model and introducing new queries. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SWIFTER through its application in discovering concepts related to the COVID-19 pandemic and also provide examples of its usage in conceptual modeling.

This paper presents an unsupervised approach to analyzing the natural variability in the timing of conversations through a data-driven method called deep neural clustering (DNC). Utilizing a broad range of acoustic features that capture speech rhythm, speech rate, and overall energy, we investigate the impact of supervising the feature extraction process and explore the performance of six distinct neural network architectures across different clustering scenarios. Our findings show that a simple, efficient network called Double Wide DNC achieves the best results, especially when incorporating a supervised feature vector. Building on recent advances in unsupervised clustering, DNC offers an attractive solution for analyzing the synchronization patterns in spoken dialogue. Its high performance across multiple tasks, including the detection and production of disordered speech, makes it an ideal research tool for investigating speech rhythm. Furthermore, we propose a novel application for disordered speech created through the synchronization of healthy speakers' timing patterns, dubbed "harmonic voice." This new voice is generated by clustering speech segments based on rhythm rather than acoustic properties, yielding promising results in creating ordered, coherent vocal expressions.

I'm pleased to introduce RCSEDv2, a comprehensive online platform built with Python and Bootstrap frameworks, which enables users to generate various data visualization tools, including 1D, 2D, 3D spectral maps and plots, as well as data tables. This resource is tailored for researchers working with data to illustrate galaxy structures, such as ringed galaxies, to facilitate scientific discussions and publications. Furthermore, RCSEDv2 provides pre-built templates for creating sample plots, allowing users to share and combine up to six multi-dimensional data sets. By utilizing this platform, users can generate an array of interactive and decorative visualizations, which can be displayed online or offline. A downloadable application and a web-hosted version (rcsedv2.host) are available for offline use; the web-hosted version offers a range of pre-created examples.

Temporal action segmentation, specifically the task of unsupervised temporal action segmentation, poses significant challenges in web-mined data with poor performance due to action ambiguity and lack of labeling. A crucial factor in this task is interpreting dense action sequences from various sources. Existing methods primarily rely on pre-built action action similarity models which are limited. Additionally, they fail to leverage co-occurring actions and class-imbalanced data common in web-mined temporal action data, hindering accurate segmentation. Our proposed Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP) method addresses these challenges by developing an adaptable action similarity model utilizing dense video sequence differences, incorporating co-occurring actions, and balancing class imbalance through a novel transfer learning technique. Results show that SSCAP outperforms existing unsupervised methods on established evaluation benchmarks.

We investigate the existence of hidden-charm pentaquark states, focusing on their production and decay mechanisms. Using the commutation relations of the $SU(3)$ algebra, we create the relevant operators and derive relevant Feynman rules for their application. Our results include the prediction of possible dominant decay modes, such as $\Sigma_c^{*+} \gamma$ and $\Lambda_b \to \Lambda_{c; b} plus a meson$, and the analysis of their properties, including narrowness and stability under strong interactions. The predicted decay properties align with the findings of the $\Lambda_c^+ \pi^- $ and $J/ \psi$ puzzles, and our research also sheds light on the properties of possible $SU(3)$ multiplets, including anti-decuplet and anti-septet charmonoid states. The proposed research may lead to significant breakthroughs in understanding exotic hadrons at relevant experiments, such as the PANDA and BESIII collaborations.

Current educational frameworks used in testing courses prioritize hands-on learning and practical skills, but did you know they might not effectively evaluate a student's understanding of testing techniques? The problem with hands-on learning lies in its reliance on observing practical outcomes, rather than the theoretical foundations, which can lead to discrepancies between what students learn in practice and what they actually understand. In software testing, this issue is particularly challenging because theoretical testing methods often involve analyzing sequences of events and understanding complex temporal relationships between them. The difficulty of accurately assessing students' knowledge of such intricate concepts using only traditional methods highlights the need for a more structured approach to testing and a better understanding of the limitations of hands-on learning. Given the complexities of testing techniques and the challenges that come with evaluating students' understanding of them, we suggest that inquiry-based assessment offers a more reliable way to test students' knowledge. The proposed methodology integrates active learning techniques to modify or eliminate existing testing tools and procedures, aiming to improve teaching effectiveness by leveraging technology to assess not only what students learn, but also how they learn it. By incorporating inquiry-based assessment methods, we can provide more reliable academic feedback, recognize students' talents, and adjust teaching techniques based on individual needs. Our goal is to offer a more comprehensive academic support in testing education, recognizing that learning involves more than just memorization, but also requires understanding, insight, and critical thinking. The quality of academic teaching, in turn, depends on the quality of academic assessment.

Domain adaptation, a challenging issue in deep learning, occurs when a model performs poorly on a task due to differences between its original and new data sources. Traditional approaches, requiring access to the original domain, are impractical due to storage and data protection issues. To overcome this, we propose a novel, source-free domain adaptation method that only needs the original training data's architecture and some related information. By creating a high-level, source-agnostic knowledge framework and allowing it to be transferred between domains, we can replicate the original training's characteristics in the target domain. A preliminary test has demonstrated that this technique can reproduce the original model's performance in the target domain, and even outperforms using the original domain's data.

This report provides a review of Gas Core Reactors (GCRs) as a primary system for nuclear propulsion systems, meant to serve as a basis for discussions at the 2022 INUP conference. The report includes discussions of how various GCR configurations affect nuclear power generation, thermal energy conversion, and propulsion system performance. It also covers key areas and the challenges associated with each component, concluding with potential paths for future research and development in these areas.

This study develops and explains a novel neural network design for particle physics research. Its core function is to identify the location of particle interactions within large-area detectors used in astroparticle experiments. Key aspects that influence interaction location detection in these studies are taken into consideration in this research. A neural network model inspired by medical image analysis is created and tested using simulated data from a massive solar flare. A thorough examination of various deep learning approaches based on their performance, reliability, and physical underlying principles is presented.

The study of heavily line-dumped absorption lines in the spectra of cool stars and brown dwarfs is crucial for analyzing their atmospheric properties. However, extensive line lists are needed to accurately model these systems. The new database, EXOPLINES, provides extensive molecular absorption cross-sections and a related line list known as EXOPLINES_L lines. Specifically, it includes key molecules in the atmospheres of cool stars and giant exoplanets, such as Ti, Fe, Mn, Na, K, Cs, Rb, and C. For these species, it covers the relevant temperature ranges and pressures in their respective atmospheric contexts. The data includes a comprehensive line list of the abundant elements, enabling detailed analysis of optical spectra from 5000 Angstroms to 1.1 microns. The EXOPLINES database is a valuable resource for in-depth analysis of the atmospheres of cool stars and giant exoplanets.

Answer Set Programming employs a non-monotonic reasoning framework based on logic programs and their associated models, known as answer sets. In the realm of Answer Set Programming, various efforts have focused on integrating external knowledge sources. There are two primary approaches to achieving this integration: one involves translating the external knowledge into a logic program, with its associated semantics, and the other entails utilizing a discipline that facilitates a logic programming groundness axiomatization. The groundness axiomatization technique generates logic programs based on existing knowledge, representing a novel method of integration distinct from the translation approach. Although both techniques allow for the representation of both deductive and non-deductive information, they have differing applications and fundamental aspects. In our study, we have identified and clarified the inherent principles of the groundness axiomatization technique, providing a formal definition and a companion tool developed to generate grounding axioms according to specified parameters. Furthermore, we have illustrated the usage of this technique in tackling machine learning and data analysis challenges.

In various quantum information theories, being an abundant resource enables certain tasks. Our investigation focuses on a general theory of abundant resources, which we call 'universal'. It encompasses many established theories, such as entanglement and non-signalling resources, which are built on the concept of extensive abstraction. We introduce a fundamental principle for these resources, referred to as the 'initial law principle', which stipulates that a state with the lowest possible abundance is given by the uniform distribution across all possible states of the theory. This principle enables us to establish rigorous systematics and mathematical structure for such resource theories. In entanglement theory, we demonstrate that our definition of abundant resources leads to the well-known monotone increase of mutual information, while in signalling theory, it enables the determination of abundant resources for any given local dimension. Our study also introduces a higher-level mathematical structure for these resource theories, which includes a pre-order for abundant resources. This work primarily addresses theoretical purposes but may also lead to new applications within quantum physics and related areas.

This chapter introduces a novel approach to assessing data by analyzing its statistical properties, which can be derived directly from theoretical models or measured from experimental data. The goal is to identify key characteristics of a dataset, determine its consistency with established models, and uncover any deviations or anomalies. The text focuses on parameters quantifying data concentration and pattern regularity, and their ability to inform model selection and reveal inherent structural aspects of the data. To account for potential outliers, a robust method is employed, similar to the one used in information-theoretic techniques. The text presents theoretical concepts alongside empirical examples and practical guidelines for implementing the methods.

We explore multivariate time series with heavy-tailed distributions that are not drawn from the stable distribution family. In particular, we investigate $p$-exponential distributions with $p<2$, and this class of heavy-tailed distributions is extensively researched in recent literature. Our focus is on a single observation from a defined index, and we aim to estimate specific quantiles and the mean absolute deviation between the mean values of recent and all historical observations. Our method combines a recent work by Agostino, Catania, and Loukus (2022) with the wild bootstrap technique for confidence interval construction. Our findings also extend the work by Loukus and Sarafoglou (2021) to the multivariate setting. Through simulated data, we compare our method's performance to established techniques like the MEST of Politis and Trivello-Bozzi (2017) and the bootstrap method of Calandoni and Franchetti-Gazzola (2020-21), showcasing stronger finite-sample performance for our method in terms of asymptotic consistency. Our proposed methods are applied to the analysis of extreme stock returns.

A novel approach to designing and decoding quantum low-density parity-check codes is presented. These codes are constructed by arranging induced quantum errors as independent binary linear equations with efficient random solutions. This structured encoding enables decoders to solve the resulting equations within linear time, yielding significant advantages in performance and decoding time. Our experimental results show the improved robustness and efficiency of these codes in both random and malicious interference environments compared to conventional LDPC codes in classical computing.

A controlling set of size $|S|$ for a graph $G$ and radius $r$ is a subset $S$ of $G$ such that for every vertex $v$ in $G$, there is a subset $B$ of $r$ neighbors of $v$ that intersects with $S$. A graph is considered to have a controlling set of size $|S|$ if the size of $S$ equals $|S|$ and it can be found in a time complexity of $\Omega(|G| + |S|^2). A graph is considered to have a controlling set of size $|S|$ if the size of $S$ equals $|S|$ and it can be found in a time complexity of $\Omega(|G| + |S|^2)$. A graph is considered to have a 2-colorable bipartite backbone when it can be divided into bipartite subgraphs such that the subgraph containing the neighbors of $v$ is of size at most $\Omega(\log |G|)$ for every $v$. A graph with a path of at most $\Omega(\log |G|)$ between any two of its vertices is considered a sparse graph. A graph with a path of at most $\Omega(\log |G|)$ between any two of its vertices is considered a sparse graph. Theoretical models forecast that irregular materials with a complex structure have a tendency towards higher-order topological properties.  However, the connection between these properties and their irregular component has remained unclear. In our study, we examined the impact of a random surface defect on a 3D topological insulator and a 2D topological insulator with an irregular edge. Using a combination of theoretical and simulation approaches, we found that the disorder on the surface could trigger higher-order topological properties even in clean systems. The extent of these properties was limited by the disorder itself and we identified specific criteria for the disorder to exhibit specific properties. The random disorder model we developed can be applied to predict the effects of defects in irregular materials. Our study also reveals that the surface disorder can be characterized through the spatial distribution of delayed surface states. The coexistence of these states with their interior counterparts illustrates the importance of accounting for surface irregularities when modeling these complex systems.

In 2016, the Large Hadron Collider discovered a signal of weakly-interacting dark matter particles, after years of intensive searches. This breakthrough not only validated numerous theoretical models but also offered relevant constraints on the properties of the hypothesized dark matter particles. Simultaneously, findings from LHC searches across various channels have provided further limitations on the parameters governing the dark matter particles' behavior. Combining these conclusions, researchers have obtained a more comprehensive understanding of the theoretical frameworks. This knowledge will be explored further in my presentation, where I will share the most recent results from LHC searches for dark matter, based on data collected during 2017, and derive the most stringent constraints on the parameters relevant to the theoretical models studied.

Automated analysis of biological structures via confocal microscopy relies on expertly trained biologists, who manually classify 3D cell categories such as cells, cells in division, or cells with damage. Current strategies for cell classification in biological structures involve preparing a dataset of typical cell examples and training a neural network to identify rare and unusual instances. However, standard training methods fail to effectively engage with unusual patterns on the boundary of its defined categories due to a tendency towards representing typical examples more accurately. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a unique training approach, called Bright Field Neural Visualization, that incorporates a stylized representation where regions outside of the focused category are represented by a neutral background. This method helps the network distinguish its focused category from neutral areas while allowing it to recognize neutral areas in relation to the focused category's structure. This approach has proven successful by simulating the way biologists visually examine microscope images.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2021 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

We investigate three heavenly N=1 supercosymplectic first-order differential equations with two variables. These equations have notable solutions that exhibit complete integrability due to their explicit expander functions for all N=1 cosymplectic structures' variations. When considering certain reductions, the known systems of Klimshach, Galerkin, and Green-Tulczyk equations emerge as specific instances. Certain combinations of these reduced systems display an intriguing self-generated square inhomogeneity. A corresponding square to the fully integrable system with N=2 cosymplectic structure does, however, lack this property when solved through square integrability. Furthermore, we identify and utilise a supercosymplectic flat connection that functions in conjunction with a novel N=1 supercosymplectic structure, referred to as "black", to efficiently apply colour-kinematics correspondence to four-graviton amplitudes analysis.

A rare event called a piston surge occurs when a disturbance driven by a coronal mass ejection travels through the lower solar atmosphere, preserving its shape and properties. Several recent studies have explored this phenomenon using the LOFAR radio telescope, but they have been hindered by limited spatial resolution. A new investigation employs high-cadence and short-baseline LOFAR observations of a coronal jet to assess how frequently piston surges occur in association with coronal mass ejections. It has been discovered that piston surges are relatively infrequently associated with CMEs, specifically occurring in less than a quarter of cases. Moreover, it appears that piston surges often disappear before reaching the lowest observable frequency recorded during the observations, implying significant low-frequency absorption. A model combining a hydrodynamic piston shock and a power-law distribution of electron densities across the jet successfully accounts for the observed radio emission, including expectations for higher-frequency observations.

In light of recent findings from the Fermilab experiment, discussing the likelihood of certain irregularities in neutrino oscillations and an enhanced W boson mass as predicted by the two Higgs doublet model is appropriate, is necessary. We focus specifically on probability assessment concerning a particular type of irregularity in neutrino oscillations, known as flavour nonclosed (FNC) events and an earlier enhancement of the W boson mass, this is done by computing and presenting the posterior probabilities of FC and ΔM_W values, following their measurement by Fermilab. We investigate the possible impacts of certain global signs, such as an anomalous antimuon magnetic moment, and whether certain global signs can coexist. We explore the implications of our findings for model building within the two Higgs doublet model (NHDM).

The random whirlpool model in three dimensions has been developed using functional probabilistic differential equations. This 3D model is derived from a global statistical analysis of the two-dimensional whirlpool model. The transition to the 3D model was driven by a method called "add a friend, remove a constraint." The results include a fully explicit form of the 3D model, and it has been demonstrated that the two-dimensional model is an emergent phenomenon arising from the three-dimensional dynamics. Additionally, practical implications and scope for further exploration of the models are considered.

The boson sampling experiment starts with a specific quantum system that generates a state vector containing a particular type of correlation when interacting with a specific Hamiltonian. This correlation manifests as entanglement when measuring certain parts of the system. The amount of entanglement present provides information on the m-dimensional block of the system's state vector, referred to as the 'boson sampling matrix,' which consists of the coefficients for combinations of bosons. By theoretically examining the entanglement of these matrices, the study demonstrates that higher entanglement corresponds to shorter boson sampling paths. The amount of entanglement also determines the sampling rate and precision, with maximum entanglement resulting in single-shot sampling outcomes, and minimum entanglement leading to Poisson-distributed frequencies of multiple bosons. The study further shows that for small groups of bosons, the boson sampling matrix is close to a specific type of quantum system known as the Peres-Werner matrix, which has distinct correlations based on boson frequency. The sample frequencies for these matrices follow a specific pattern and can be utilized for partial quantum computation.

Using deep Q-networks, an agent can learn to navigate and interact with various simulated virtual environments. However, real-world applications in life science often involve analyzing short-term data collected through diverse methods. The deep Q-network may struggle with short-term tasks due to its large action space, including actions like time series prediction, sequence alignment, and feature extraction. To improve upon this limitation, we developed a novel variant of the deep Q-network, reducing its memory constraints and enhancing its ability to handle short-term tasks efficiently. The improved model successfully applies itself to tasks such as predicting short-term time series, comparing DNA sequences, and learning to extract relevant features from various conditions. Its performance surpasses the traditional deep Q-network, with our full implementation available on GitHub at https://github.com/timengwan/BRHDQ.

We've developed a theoretical framework to examine how complex neural networks process uncertain information and form subconscious hypotheses about their surroundings. By applying this theory, we've shown that certain types of artificial neural networks, specifically those with interconnected structures (recurrent networks), can and should form these hypotheses even when they don't always have the information they need. This perspective, rooted in the concept of "beliefs", offers a unique understanding of the learning and decision-making processes of complex systems, especially those that are unable to confirm their assumptions. By calculating how likely certain events are based on past observations, we've demonstrated that these "beliefs" can take the form of probability distributions. Even in normal operating conditions, we've discovered that parts of the system may not have access to the information necessary to explain its behavior, suggesting the existence of "hidden" states. To determine how to identify these hidden states and verify our theory, we've developed a method that combines the process of forming hypotheses with the process of eliminating options, specifically cross-entropy minimization and belief testing. When we simulated the system to confirm our approach, we found that parts of the system may and do develop their own internal models of their surroundings, even when they only have partial information.

There's been significant interest in detecting human actions in videos, specifically in cases where only vague labels are available, such as a person performing some activity without specifying the activity itself. Existing approaches use external information like word embeddings to represent context but this only accounts for linguistic context and ignores visual cues from videos. On the other hand, labelled videos often show a clear context as a background. Our method takes in weakly-guided activity labels and identifies relevant context by learning from neighbouring instances in a feature graph. Our innovative self-supervised method trains a graph convolutional network to distinguish between context and background, promoting generalisation to unseen situations. In contrast to prior work, our focus isn't on word embeddings but rather on learning context visually grounded in video data. Our technique doesn't require manual labelling of context and is compatible with existing action detection methods. Experimental results show that by capturing visual context, our method outperforms current state-of-the-art action detectors on activity detection and when combined with existing action detectors, it overall surpasses current performance.

The 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, held in conjunction with the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, drew participants from a diverse background, producing an impressive 710 submissions across three tracks. Our analysis of this challenge reveals new insights, notably that reliance on pre-trained models impairs performance and that our official evaluation process fails to accurately forecast competition results. A thorough examination of top solutions sheds light on effective techniques, while the lack of challenge in two tracks indicates areas requiring further development. We are releasing the dataset for future research purposes.

The subject matter of this manuscript consists of three projects which examine spatio-temporal irregularities in parabolic equations, focusing on internal and external metastability phenomena in the context of mathematical modeling. Irregularities occurring internally are studied using the theory of homogenization, while an asymptotic-degeneracy approach is developed to investigate metastability. Moreover, the manifestation of irregularities at the equation's boundary is also considered, with a contribution of a new type made in this area.

The recent research article titled "Computation of Nuclear Substance in the Presence of Intense Magnetic Field using the Local Coupled Channel Method" explores the impact of strong magnetic fields on the properties of nuclei. A novel approach using the Local Coupled Channel Method has been developed to describe this phenomenon. Utilizing this method, investigators have calculated the energy spectra of $^{16}$O for different orientations relative to the magnetic field and found that the intensity of the magnetic field influences the binding energy of the nucleons significantly. Additionally, the study examines the spatial distribution of the nucleons in the nucleus and its relationship with the orientation of the magnetic field.

In distributed neural network training, optimal performance and efficiency are often balanced by a tradeoff between communication expense and data security. To address this, we have created an innovative approach that utilizes secure two-party protocols to enable secure and efficient training while minimizing communication cost. This approach replaces expensive MPSoT operations with cheaper APoT, achieving significant improvements in scalability and efficiency. Using high-performance servers and fast network connections, we have optimized the training process by increasing the size of data batches before compression and encryption. Our results show that this optimization can reduce communication cost by five times while maintaining performance. Additionally, we have developed a comprehensive framework for secure neural network training that provides flexible data management and protocol configuration, enabling us to achieve top performance and efficiency in training using 256GPUs, 16 servers and high-speed network connections.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex has been compiled by combining the observations from three space missions: FIMS, FUSE, and GALEX. These combined data offer a detailed insight into the UV radiation environment of the region, spanning approximately 500 parsec in diameter, at a resolution equivalent to 15 arcminutes or 12.5 parsecs. The UV intensity within the complex is highly anisotropic, largely due to molecular clouds obstructing the path of the radiation stream. A moderate far-ultraviolet background intensity of around 40-50 Rayleighs is present in the region, primarily resulting from the blocking of nearby star clusters by small clouds. The UV radiation environment is observed to be dynamic, with stars influencing the surrounding dust grains through photon-molecule interactions. The star counts in the region have also shown a disconnection between the UV source density and the number of young stellar objects in specific molecular clouds, indicating possible scattering due to ambient clouds in some cases and a correlation in another. Finally, the UV radiation environment of the region appears to predate the formation of the spiral arm complex, as evidenced by the presence of CO emission signals in the region.

Structured tables in documents enable effective information retrieval by offering an organized layout. The primary challenge in table extraction lies in overcoming the diverse formats in which tables are presented within documents. In this research, we examine the table extraction task within the context of structured documents, presenting an innovative method that leverages Graph Neural Networks. Our approach involves a four-stage process: breaking down the document into individual graph nodes and edges using text zones and interline spaces, followed by a graph construction phase that identifies nodes belonging to the same row. We then employ Graph Neural Networks to distinguish rows and columns within the graph, and finally utilize an attention mechanism to consolidate the representation of each cell. Our solution has been extensively tested using the PubLayNet dataset, yielding exceptional results in performance benchmarking.

This research delves into complex multi-stage games characterized by uncertainty, specifically those defined by dynamic finite state-matrix games with sequential arms-length agreements and hidden player types. Each player in such games has two distinct cognitive capabilities: the ability to first make educated guesses about their fellow players' hidden characteristics, followed by the ability to adapt their strategy in response to perceived situations. We begin by examining a specific variant of this game, where players are subject to specific limitations in their initial information regarding their fellow players' types, thereby allowing us to identify distinct strategic layers. We then establish a specific variant of these games as a class of Markov Decision Processes, thereby enabling us to apply optimal policy approach to gain insight into the specific cognitive capabilities of the players, including their ability to make educated guesses and adapt to perceived situations. We then compare the effectiveness of both cognitive capabilities, showing that while they are distinct, they are however interchangeable. This specific variant of such games also reveals that when players have limited ability to adapt their strategy in response to perceived situations, those using an optimal policy approach to this specific variant of such games are more inclined to make educated guesses about their fellow players' types, whereas those using an optimal policy approach to the general variant of such games are more inclined to adapt their strategy in response to perceived situations.

Population assessments based on satellite imagery can be challenging due to limitations in data accessibility and the technical expertise required for processing. This study focuses on applying autonomous survey techniques using drones and on-foot sensors for population estimation in rural areas. Two potential approaches using multi-spectral and synthetic aperture radar imaging are presented, along with an evaluation of their effectiveness in diverse environmental conditions. Given the variability in terrain and weather, our recommended strategy involves combining drone and sensor data through a machine learning method to generate accurate population estimates. This approach is found to be feasible, efficient, and productive in this context.

In private information systems, an untrusted server stores user data, and users can submit queries to retrieve specific user information, such as IDs. To maintain user privacy, the server cannot access the full user dataset, but it can still respond to queries by guessing which users are involved. To address this issue, researchers have proposed the concept of "hiding" or "private" predicates that conceal a subset of user data at the server, allowing the server to respond to queries without learning the user identities. A particular type of private predicate known as an "E-member Filter" enables the server to guess which users are not part of a query when the server itself cannot access the user dataset. A new innovation in this research introduces a concept called "False Positive Free", indicating a specific probability threshold where the probability of an incorrect server guess is essentially zero. To address this, the researchers proposed an "FPF E-member Filter", a particular type of private predicate that ensures a reduced probability of an incorrect server guess, and a new construction that achieves this, first for a specific type of data set known as "d-arrays", and then extending this for more complex data sets known as "M-arrays", consisting of a series of "d-arrays". By achieving this construction, the researchers were able to demonstrate that a specific type of private predicate known as "private sets" is not required in order to achieve "FPF" with an added property of being "better than the

We theoretically examined a process known as laser-induced three-body recombination in a gas of bosonic Rydberg atoms. The interaction with a variable-frequency laser field causes the atoms to transition between having zero or one rotational quanta of excitation. The resulting recombination products are likely to be in a molecular state or a superposition of atomic and molecular states, especially anatomic states, which is an optimal condition for creating spin-orbit coupled molecular states. The molecular bond length and the overall wave function amplitude are found to be sensitive to the frequency and intensity of the laser field. The strength of the spin-orbit coupling can be adjusted by modifying the laser frequency or intensity. The ideal parameter range for creating spin-orbit coupled states is identified as being within the micrometer bond length scale and a specific intensity range that depends on the atomic species in question.

The study presents an extension of the smooth particle hydrodynamics (SPH) formulation to tackle multi-phase fluid-structure interactions at multiple scales. The efficient interaction between fluid and solid phases is ensured through a strong coupling technique. The solid structures in our model can be modeled as a collection of particles with either analytical or particle-based constitutive models that account for material properties. The multi-scale approach in our SPH framework for fluid dynamics incorporates different kernel sizes for fluid and solid phases, respectively. Additionally, our method incorporates unique properties such as the pressure-free boundary condition, a dynamic boundary condition, and boundary conditions for the volume averaged process. The implementation of these methods allows for full dynamic simulation of fluid and solid interactions while minimizing computations by only resolving the fluid phase at a higher resolution. As a result, our approach achieves significant speed-up in computational efficiency without sacrificing accuracy. The methodology is validated in this research by demonstrating several benchmark tests that demonstrate its capabilities in simulating fluid-structure interactions at different scales and complexity levels, in particular, the Rayleigh-Taylor instability, a floating flexible cylinder in a quiescent ambient fluid, flow around rigid or flexible fixed-bottom cylinders under various cross-flow load cases, and lastly, a sailing boat with a rigid top-mast. The simulations show excellent agreement with established multi-phase FSI methods in the scientific literature as well as with experimental measurements available for two of the test cases.

Artificial intelligence's rapid advancement has brought new computational challenges due to the limited speed of electrical data transfer between devices, including computers. The transfer of data between the brain and a computer's hardware can cause delays, hinder real-time data processing, and increase the energy consumption of complex neural networks. The limitations of current hardware, including power consumption, speed, and storage, must be addressed to develop more efficient neural systems. Researchers have proposed quantum neural networks to resolve these issues, potentially allowing for significant optimizations. Specifically, a new learning algorithm, quantum unmonitored and instructed learning, was applied to superconducting quantum processors, resulting in enhanced performance. The experiment demonstrated improved accuracy and reduced training time, indicating that the energy required to train the network decreased exponentially with the number of training samples. The successful implementation of this algorithm on a quantum hardware substrate opens the door for various instruction-based learning techniques and a range of applications in biology, chemistry, and physics. The results suggest that adapting current AI systems to the limitations of quantum processors can yield substantial gains in speed, efficiency, and effectiveness. The experiment also showed that the EUIL algorithm can efficiently learn from data without constant monitoring, a capability that could be important for autonomous learning systems. The research further expanded the possibilities of quantum neural networks, bringing us closer to developing more advanced artificial intelligence systems that harness the power of quantum computing.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's pushed to its limits. In other words, it can only safely be used for a small range of voice tones before the speech starts sounding unnatural. We've developed a way to improve FastPitch's ability to control pitch without altering its voice characteristics. We've also implemented a method to stretch the voice to new, never-heard tones in just a few seconds, which significantly expands the range of tones that FastPitch can safely use. Experiments with both normal and extremely loud speech showed that our method is timbre-consistent and more reliable than a similar but more complex model. We've also released our modified model, which we call FastPitch Pro, so that others can use it for their own speech synthesis projects.

This research focuses on solving spatiottemporal reasoning challenges by employing instance-based learning techniques utilizing Deep Learning methods. A novel multi-hop reasoning approach, integrated within a Visual Question Answering framework, is introduced. By leveraging this approach, answers to complex questions requiring multi-step logical deductions can be accurately identified. Moreover, to enhance learning with reasoning, we create a diverse dataset of spatiotemporal reasoning questions and conduct experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method across various benchmarks.

This research presents predictions for producing double electrons or muons in conjunction with two $b$-quarks through the s-channel in the Standard Model, using the Feynman diagram technique. We find that the ratio of muon to electron yields is approximately 0.020. We also provide an expression to estimate $W$ boson mass changes in terms of $b$-quark kinematic properties for this process. For experimental purposes where the leading background may have a similar characteristics profile as the $W$ plus two $b$ event, a specific observant called $i$ ($i$ range 1 to 17) can be used to estimate $\Delta p_t^W$ with resolution $R_{pt}$, even if $W$ momentum is not directly known. $\Delta p_t^W$ can also be used to constrain beyond the Standard Model events.

Remote-controlled vehicles known as telepresence robots have gained attention in various fields, such as healthcare and education, due to their interactive capabilities. A crucial aspect in these applications is the Quality of Interaction (QoI) which the existing methods fail to address effectively. A key challenge in measuring QoI is the lack of a participatory evaluation approach, making it an unsolved problem in the field. To address this, we developed an adaptable framework for evaluating QoI that can be applied across different applications. This framework consists of three main components: (i) a remote-viewing comfort scale to measure visual interaction quality, (ii) a summated control difficulty scale to assess the ease of vehicle control, and (iii) an in-depth interview protocol to gain insight into users' overall experience. The framework's effectiveness was demonstrated in a real-world study conducted with 16 participants who used the vehicles under different lighting and network conditions. The study showed that our framework provides more accurate measurements than self-reporting and can also identify users' preferences and discomforts. The framework has been made available to the research community, and our results highlight its practical applications in enhancing telepresence robot design and usability.

In the realm of intelligence research, examining what causes variations in cognitive abilities and emotions, and how these factors manifest in different populations, is a critical aspect. Conventional studies using mean separations often fall short, as they don't accurately reflect the effects in question. On the other hand, multilevel models offer a more realistic representation of these phenomena, incorporating variability at individual and group levels, yet can be computationally demanding and require advanced statistical knowledge. We propose an alternative approach, called Bayesian Hierarchical Linear Analysis (BHLA), which is an efficient and principled method for this type of analysis. Unlike MLPMC, a related Bayesian method, BHLA is characterized by the absence of convergence issues, a more straightforward posterior distribution, and better diagnostic tools. We present BHLA, along with a Bayesian spin-j 1/2 model, to demonstrate its capabilities and showcase its applicability in cognitive mathematics.

We examine a game known as Mafia, in which a defined number of players, $N$, includes both innocent roles, known as civilians, and malicious roles, referred to as Mafias. The Mafias possess the ability to remain hidden during voting activities. Consequently, any civilian role voted off by the players as part of a public vote may be eliminated by the Mafias through private assassination. Due to this combined threat from both public and private means of elimination, the survivors face a higher mortality rate. In particular, any civilian role, denoted as $c$, faces a mortality rate that is the sum of the public vote ratio, $\frac p N$, and the private assassination probability, denoted as $q$. In this context, the public vote ratio and private assassination probability represent the respective fractions of Mafias and non-Mafas among the remaining survivors. In contrast, the mortality rate of a Mafia is solely based on the public vote ratio. By simulating this game with varying numbers of survivors, $N$, and Mafias, denoted as $m$, we investigate its relevance in an infinite survivor population. Our findings reveal that the relative fractions of survivors consisting of Mafias and non-Mafas enable a more precise assessment of the combined threat from public and private forms of elimination. Our research indicates that the relative fractions of survivors are less heavily impacted by the presence of Mafias compared to scenarios where only public elimination threats are present. The formation of giant planets through a core accretion theory involves the conversion of solid material into gas due to gravitational influence. However, the interaction between a planet and its surrounding gas disk can drive gas accumulation, increasing the planet's mass. This study investigates how gas accumulation influences the formation of planets and modifies the surrounding disk structure. We analyzed a type of planetary pair, called pseudo-resonant twins, located near the orbit of a massive star. These planets are unique in that they can attract and retain a significant amount of gas, significantly increasing their mass. Using a state-of-the-art computer code that simulates planetary and disk evolution, we analyzed the development of these planetary systems over time. We found that the thinner the disk, the more effective gas accumulation becomes, leading to a significant increase in the planets' mass. This increased gas pressure causes the planets to experience a slower rate of migration, extending their lifetime in the disk. This evolution leads to smaller, compact disks that eventually disappear when the planets reach their maximum mass, typically around 5-7 years old in the context of rapid gas accumulation. However, when we varied the planets' initial positions, their final masses remained constant, suggesting that their mass is determined independently of their birth conditions and instead influenced by their concurrent gas accumulation.

Theoretical simulations have shown that an unusual form of electronic conduction exists in a layer of nanotubes with a specific arrangement, facilitated through the use of light as a medium. This process involves the transfer of electrons between different nanotubes through the use of light to support electronic conduction. An experimental study has now demonstrated that this phenomenon can also occur in a different configuration of nanotubes at the interface between different materials. The researchers found that this effect occurs at the interface of two types of carbon nanotubes due to the sharing of electrons and occurs through the use of light to support electronic conduction. Additionally, they have also shown that this phenomenon can be influenced by the mechanical properties of the nanotubes as they change shape in response to light. The discovery of this new electronic behavior provides further evidence that even at the microscopic level, novel electronic behaviors can occur beyond the standard band theory model that describes electronic conduction.

This research presents a novel fuzzy k-means approach to classify high-dimensional data over a fuzzy partition. Traditional fuzzy k-means algorithms have been adapted from their low-dimensional counterparts without consideration of the increased information loss in high-dimensional spaces. Consequently, the fuzzy k-means clusters may fail to optimize clustering quality. To rectify this issue, this paper develops a novel entropy-based weighted fuzzy k-means method that assigns cluster-specific weights to mitigate the negative consequences of dimensionality's influence on fuzzy k-means. In doing so, this algorithm ensures that each dimension's contribution to cluster formation is balanced across dimensions. Furthermore, this methodology can determine the optimal number of clusters automatically by analyzing the weighted intra-cluster variances. The efficacy of this approach is then verified through simulation experiments performed using artificial and real-world datasets, which reveal its superiority to conventional fuzzy k-means methods.

The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) algorithm, widely used for distributed learning, has been the subject of recent research. Experts specialize in specific subgroups within the training dataset, but its implementation has been hindered by a deadlock caused when an assignment, deemed suboptimal due to model predictive errors, is repeated infinitely. Despite being a common issue, few have addressed it in the research community. This paper presents Reliable MoE (RoME), an enhanced algorithm designed to mitigate the deadlock by introducing a built-in assignment correction mechanism. Unlike other proposals, which rely on heuristics, RoME guarantees infinite convergence and a stable rate of convergence, all while maintaining the accuracy and scalability of traditional MoE. Valido, Google Cloud's distributed training platform, has been used to test RoME in real-world conditions, showing significant improvements compared to standard MoE algorithms, as well as existing solutions like DMOE.

This research explores an extension of the theoretical framework established in earlier studies (arXiv:2009. 13215 and arXiv:2012.16512), focused on the mathematical structures expressed through symmetric polynomials. Specifically, we investigate how the intersection of union paths in the modular group that include the identity element and a particular subgroup influences these expressions. As a result, we derive formulas describing forms associated with Jacobians and a modified version of the modular group that relate to the 2-cubic theta function and a related form. Additionally, we explain how the proposed framework aligns with the principles of algebraic curves and elliptic curves, including an application related to the Token game.

Quantum gravitational effects in the early universe can lead to the disruption of global symmetry, resulting in potential birefrungent signatures due to the fluctuating boundary between space and foam. This concept is based on the hypothesis that global symmetry disruption may occur during the cosmic phase transition, such as during the EPIC era when the universe interacted with the quantum gravitational foam. A virtual particle exchange process with unbounded virtual particles causes global symmetry disruption, and the inherent polarization of gravitational waves could allow this phenomenon to be observed before the Planck era, with the E-mode polarization possibly appearing around the EPIC time frame and transitioning to noise after the reheating event following the Big Bang.

Our study presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147, captured by the AstroSat satellite's Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope. The data collection spanned approximately 21 hours, yielding FUV images of 14 FUV bright, blue-horizontal branch stars and 5 "blue hook" stars within the cluster. Using the collected data, we determined an FUV to optical color-magnitude diagram for 19 of these stars and derived a luminosity of -0.73±0.03 mag for the FUV bright sub-giant branch in the cluster. Building upon the 2002 HST photo, we established a 200,000 to 300,000 year time frame for the FUV bright FG/BG phase in the cluster. Notably, our FUV luminosity matches the primary sequence of the cluster, indicating direct hydrogen shell burning on the central regions of the initial progenitor stars. The resulting initial-to-final mass ratio for the FUV bright FG/BG stars ranges from 0.19 to 0.29. This ratio lies above the global GSS of the Milky Way (0.056) and is consistent with the effect of initial metallicity in the mass range of 2-3 solar masses. Our research also reveals a bimodal initial metal distribution for the stars in NGC 4147, with the majority (8 out of 13) having a higher initial metallicity compared to

This paper aims to develop a 'feeble b-principle' based on the notion that if a topological map from a compact orientable surface to the 2-sphere can be decorated with an integer value, then the same can be done for a similar map, except with the target changed to a 2-sphere equipped with a single north-south disk removal. We demonstrate that this principle has implications for three separate problems: proving the irreducibility of certain moduli spaces related to algebraic geometry known as moduli spaces of curves, specifically those involving the 'Mumford hypothesis'; a 'density problem' concerning topological graphs with isolated edges; and a 'transfer problem' allowing us to move from considerations of maps to surface-like surfaces to those of surface-like graphs.

Deep neural networks' transferability has garnered significant attention in the field of deep learning. Generally, it is thought that a network trained on one dataset can be utilized as a feature extractor for another, with similar or dissimilar categories, and that ongoing training can refine features tailored to the specific dataset. However, we challenge these assumptions in this study. Our findings suggest that these two forms of transferability are not simultaneous and cannot be concurrently achieved. Furthermore, we argue that the process of training a pre-trained network on a new dataset can actually hinder its transferability compared to initiating training from scratch. Our recommendations for optimizing transferability include disabling momentum-based optimization and commencing training without pre-training the network. These findings present new perspectives on the transferability of deep neural networks, raising the possibility of further investigation into the underlying mechanisms of this phenomenon.

The faster and more evenly spread information travels, especially during emergencies, when multiple sources need to be quickly informed of critical events. The speed of information dissemination in undirected networks is profoundly affected by its structure. We show that in networks composed of communities, the rate at which information spreads is directly influenced by the tightness of these communities and their relative sizes. By utilizing a stochastic model of message passing, we derived this outcome. The model confirms that network architecture significantly impacts the dissemination rate, thereby implying the existence of an optimal network structure for the fastest information dissemination.

The unique characteristic or distinguishability of a geometric object, particularly a point, can be measured in terms of its unique features under different types of transformations. The concept of quantitative distinctiveness, first introduced by Gackere et al., helps identify unique features of an object and their corresponding metrics. Building on this concept, we have developed a new criterion, inspired by unique geodesics, to measure the distinctiveness of manifolds, including those with positive or zero sectional curvature. The effectiveness of this new criterion has been demonstrated in the classification of locally symmetric complex surfaces. This method also led to a revalidation of previous results by Gackere et al. and an extension of the unique geodesic criterion by Canzani-Ullrich to include unique transformation sequences.

The time-domain standard perturbation model is commonly used to investigate the timing accuracy of optical time domain and related systems, however it only accounts for discrete time increments of $T_s$ and overlooks the inherent non-uniformity and continuity of the channel, which hampers assessing the impact on, for example, optical time domain systems utilizing frequency domain compensation techniques. In this paper, we derive a modified perturbation model that provides a more precise description of the effects of random channel distortions on discrete-phase signals in systems lacking amplification, in terms of mean error and variance. By comparing these models, we also examine scenarios where the random channel is characterized by a raised cosine amplitude spectrum. The results obtained will contribute to the development of enhanced timing recovery techniques for various communication systems.

The widespread adoption of smart devices has led to a significant increase in malicious attacks, particularly those targeting the devices' underlying Operating Systems. In the case of Android, a notable characteristic is its "evasion" strategy, which allows malware to avoid being detected by Anti-Virus software by modifying its behavior, thus remaining undetected. In this study, we examined a subset of studies focused on evasion assaults within Android's operating system, with a goal of identifying commonalities among these attacks. The results of this investigation reveal the kinds of evasion attacks employed, their prevalence, and patterns, as well as the frequent utilization of specific evasion techniques that contribute to evasion attacks. Notably, our research found an absence of scholarly efforts devoted to a comprehensive analysis of evasion assaults on Android OS. Therefore, we intend to utilize our analysis as a foundation for future research on this subject.

Deep learning's broad impact has led to a surge in varied, specialized models, prompting a corresponding increase in custom tools for each model type. However, this trend complicates the process of training these models, particularly when attempting to compare results or optimize model hyperparameters. To streamline model training, we suggest developing a unified framework: Ozy. This framework, represented as a block diagram, is a highly adaptable tool for incorporating many model types. We present a universal implementation of its scheme in the Python language, referred to as Ozy: a universal orchestration vessel. This package is versatile enough to incorporate new model types simply by replicating existing blocks, allowing for the efficient inclusion of novel methods. A comprehensive guide to using Ozy, along with the associated code and executable demos, is accessible online at the provided URL.

In moderate-strong magnetic fields, a unique reentrant phase of electron-electron interaction is discovered in the fifth fractional quantum Hall state, distinguished from the well-known Pfaffian phase by distinct energy scaling behaviors. Utilizing a combination of analytical and numerical methods, the reentrant phase's underlying symmetry and structure have been found to be equivalent to that of Pfaffian, but with a distinct particle-hole transformed form of the ground state. Our findings demonstrate that in the fifth fractional quantum hall state, a well-known phase of interaction, namely the Pfaffian phase, can be transformed into an unconventional phase, known as the reentrant phase, by adjusting the strength of electron-electron interaction, which is a phenomenon that cannot be observed in the lowest energy fractional quantum hall state. This discovery is due to the occurrence of a phase transition, known as the bosonic collective-field crossover, in high magnetic field conditions. Our study also reveals that, in general, the phase stability of the pfaffian wave function against electron-backscattering processes is governed by a certain quantitative rule. Our work also opens new pathways in the laboratory study of fractional quantum hall phases in high magnetic field conditions and utilising quantum dot engineering.

Our investigation of primordial black holes (PBHs) deviates from standard analyses by incorporating accurate equations of state from cosmological data and LIGO-Virgo events. Two critical factors are considered: the PBH mass function and density, and the characteristic black hole profile, disputed among experts. We show that earlier studies likely used an incorrect profile, the Thakurta metric, based on outdated concepts. This mistake has significant implications for our understanding of PBH cosmology. In this study, multiple profiles for characterizing PBH are presented and a novel, consistent, and simplified approach for PBH constraints is proposed. Utilizing LIGO-Virgo events, the constraints on PBH on small scales remain largely unchanged, confirming previous findings. Additionally, the impact of PBH on large-scale structures and the cosmic microwave background (CMB) is examined, and we find minimal effects of PBH on these large-scale phenomena. These results are consistent when varying the PBH mass function and density. This study provides an alternative to existing PBH studies in a more characterized environment, with an emphasis on developing a self-consistent and flexible method for PBH constraints and predictions across multiple scales.

The formation of planets through pebble accumulation is studied in a novel, non-homogeneous disk environment characterized by localized density fluctuations. In this setting, a more dense "island" in the disk enables planets to form earlier than in uniform models, with the peak of their growth in the inner island shifting to higher masses as the disk's density drops. In the later stages, a less dense "island" allows the formation of planets with broader orbits than in uniform models, with a maximum mass that doesn't rise much further with time. In an average, uniform model context, interactions between planets and their surroundings lead to the marginalization of nearby density fluctuations. However, in an environment rich in dust, where interactions between planets and their surroundings are less pronounced, the formation of planets with diverse orbital paths is possible, even in a uniform context, albeit at a slower pace. Ultimately, detailed observations of multiple planets within the same orbital path should be treated as an average over numerous birth sites, rather than a single event.

In this study, we examine two models - the *Bounded Depth Neural Network* and the *Limited Query Neural Network*, each with unique constraints. The *BDNN* is a neural network limited in its internal process but unrestricted in its parameters, whereas the *LQNN* is a neural network limited in the information it can retrieve but unrestricted in its parameters. We establish new bounds for these models, demonstrating that they can learn any target function to satisfactory accuracy, regardless of the data available, provided that the data is substantial enough. Interestingly, these models replicate the performance of the traditional overparameterized neural networks, and our results imply that the traditional neural network's ability to learn and generalize may not be a result of having enough parameters, but rather a consequence of the extensive data available. Moreover, these models shed light on a deeper learning theorem that addresses a long-standing problem in learning theory.

In a previous study, we demonstrated the existence of specific countable Boolean structures that, when expanded to include constant values from finite sets, form structures isomorphic to first-order logic theories concerning additive abelian groups of cardinality less than both countable and a power of 2. This led to the discovery of a Boolean structure with a similar property applicable to all cardinalities, particularly in the form of the Bohr subgroup of the additive group of the rational numbers. This implies that any formula in a countable language, integrated with the relation of being Bohr in models of the mentioned group, forms a definable subset within the original model. Furthermore, it was found that the structure of the natural numbers, when expanded to include constant values from finite sets, is isomorphic to a first-order theory concerning the additive abelian group of the rational numbers' Bohr subgroup. This established the Bohr subgroup's definability through first-order logic within the original model.

The dial-a-ride problem, specifically Metropolis DPR, aims to optimize routes for a fleet of vehicles serving elderly passengers in urban areas with limited parking and high transportation costs. Due to its complex nature, solving the Metropolis DPR in a near-optimal manner is a significant challenge. In response, a compact formulation is offered that reduces the problem's solution space, and a corresponding Branch-and-Trim algorithm is proposed to efficiently solve it. When tested on a widely-used instance of the metropolitan dial-a-ride problem, the proposed method produced a significantly improved solution, reducing processing time from 37 days and 8 hours in the original CPlex solver to just 0.2 seconds.

The foundation of e-commerce search systems lies in combining product data with query information. Recent years have seen considerable interest in employing pre-trained models for improved performance. However, the majority of existing models overlook e-commerce's distinct characteristics, such as hierarchical product attributes and accompanying visual content. Inspired by how humans combine query information and relevant knowledge to form search queries, we introduce the KNOMER model for multi-modal pretraining. This approach leverages knowledge graphs to define multiple information sources - query, related information, and product attributes - and employs a collaborative learning mechanism within a dual transformer framework. The KNOMER model processes these distinct features by assigning different attention mechanisms and allows the collaboration between two transformers to integrate information for enhanced representation of the learned products features. Building on the Facebook AI model architecture, we incorporate a new layer to encode the knowledge attributes and incorporate a new collarabative learning type into the model. Experimental results on a large e-commerce dataset indicate that the proposed method surpasses baseline models in several tasks and maintains real-time query processing performance. The proposed code can be accessed at https://github.com/baidu/BaiduAI_Papers

A significant issue within the neurology and psychology fields, Alzheimer's disease, which exhibits progressive memory loss, is linked closely to neurodegeneration. In the last few years, the research community has become increasingly interested in early detection and understanding the underlying causes of the condition to potentially develop effective treatments. We explore the application of a novel unsupervised learning approach, Deep InfoMax, in identifying significant features extracted from MRI images of brain tissue. By employing self-supervised methods, we aim to identify patterns and correlations that are prominent enough to distinguish between control and Alzheimer's groups, even when the data is limited. Furthermore, we train a classifier using our extracted feature set to evaluate the classification performance and advance detection capabilities.

This paper suggests a novel method to address the inherent challenge of understanding the complex variations in the depths of sentences individuals possess within the realm of language. The amount of knowledge an individual may retain is often referred to as the "cognitive level." Our approach to handling semantic variations relies on a novel interactive mechanism, incorporated within a recurrent neural network, to simulate the process of human reasoning. By allowing the model to manage cognitive levels efficiently, the interactive RNN surpasses state-of-the-art performance in the classification of sentence meanings, as demonstrated on the SICK dataset. Furthermore, our approach exhibits significant potential in developing intelligent artificial intelligence systems capable of adapting to varying human cognitive levels in applications such as natural language processing.

In a tight-binding model with nearest-neighbor hopping on a lattice with spin-orbit coupling, the effective spin-orbit interaction constant is adjusted based on the strength of on-site repulsion. For situations with strong repulsion, an increased effective spin-orbit constant is observed, which can be understood through a theoretical framework that describes the formation of local magnetic moments. These results have implications for interpreting spin-orbit coupling experiments in correlated systems, suggesting the need to consider the effects of on-site repulsion in the material.

In this research, we make the case that the shadow substance, which is essentially a new theoretical entity requiring the introduction of new dynamics, is not only permissible in conformal theory but also necessary when considering the model's dynamics, effectively eliminating the continuity of the conformal shadow operator and giving rise to a classification of the conformal spectrum based on a new physical principle derived from the breaking of the conformal symmetry. Additionally, we establish the explicit spectrum of the conformal spectrum for a specific scalar field and use the newly discovered principle to account for the phase transitions of relativistic particles.

The success of AI medical instruments depends heavily on how well they perform in real-world medical settings. Currently, reliable methods for evaluating their performance in actual medical settings are non-existent. We develop a framework based on conformal prediction that accurately assesses AI medical instruments' ability to pass medical tests under real-world medical settings. By using this framework, an AI medical instrument's predicted performance in a new medical environment can be consistently determined. Furthermore, our statistical analysis demonstrates that the developed assessment method effectively identifies underperforming medical tests. We successfully applied this framework in assessing deep neural network-based medical instruments under shift scenarios. Our study also discovered several key findings: first, we identified the minimal information required for a new medical environment to be considered a distribution shift; second, we identified the minimal conditions necessary for an AI medical instrument to be effective in a new medical setting; third, we confirmed the developed assessment method accurately identifies underperforming medical tests; and finally, we confirmed the effectiveness of a specific training approach for AI medical instruments in a new medical setting.

Many complex systems, especially proteins and nucleic acids, require an accurate modeling of electrostatic interactions to produce reliable results. However, due to the computational expense and numerical instability associated with these interactions, the traditional approach involves a parameterized shortcut that introduces an element of randomness, known as a Gaussian distribution, to approximate these interactions. The effect of this approximation can be mitigated by employing a higher accuracy approach called Poisson-Boltzmann, which considers the influence of charged groups on a molecular structure. The subsequent improvement in accuracy often results in the expansion of the area to be sampled; consequently, the time spent on less important tasks can be redirected to critical regions. In the study presented here, the focus is on the electrostatic biasing of molecular dynamics simulations of double-stranded DNA. An innovative, highly accurate method called Dielectric-Embedded Atom (DEA) is utilized to model DNA-water interactions. The results indicate that by incorporating dielectric properties and employing a refined electrostatics approach, the resulting conformational space includes a greater variety of DNA configurations, especially when the DNA is not subjected to excessive twisting forces. The resulting benefits include an increased observed period between consecutive DNA rotations and a greater variety of DNA configurations when the rotations occur more infrequently.

In the past decade, research on ANS entropy compression has been widespread, yet questions persist regarding its fundamental aspects. By focusing exclusively on this concept, this study delves into its underlying principles, uncovering novel computational mechanisms that can assess its significance in cognitive processes. Using computer-powered systems, an advanced analysis is conducted, building on initial findings that suggested its influence could last beyond initial stages of evolution. According to our results, however, this concept does not hold up to rigorous examination using advanced computational methods. It appears that subsequent stages of evolution will not be shaped by the principles of maximum entropy as previously hypothesized.

In cement-based materials, the interstitial fluid has a crucial impact on the microstructural development and electrical properties. Given that porosity accounts for a substantial fraction of the material's volume, the pore fluid plays a key role in the dielectric behavior of these systems, rendering their interpretation through the combined bulk properties of the solid and fluid phases entirely applicable. To verify this, the dielectric parameters of the pore fluid, as well as the cement paste's solidified phase, were directly measured and subsequently compared with the parameters of the same systems derived from finite element simulations based on the Stokes law. Our results demonstrate that the fluid exhibits a distinct set of dielectric parameters that differ from the solidified phase, and we have shown that the dielectric parameters of the cement paste consist of a combination of the fluid and solid phases. This knowledge could provide valuable insights into the various engineering applications of cement-based materials, such as durability and self-sensing capabilities, and may also contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying cement-based material development and malfunction.

Using an advanced version of the QCD potential model, the nature of heavy-heavy clusters observed in experimental data on charmonium and bottomonium systems is examined. Utilizing numerical solutions to the Schrodinger equation, the cross-section distribution of the initial meson's momentum and the transverse momentum of the clustered part are calculated and compared with existing experimental measurements. Results indicate that the predicted cross-section values are relatively high, ranging from 100 to 300 microbarns, in line with the observed values for the sigma (7.12 microbarns) and psi '(2) meson pairs. It's suggested that the calculated excessive cross-section values could be reduced by increasing the S-wave components at higher momentum values or by considering non-valence components, thereby providing a more accurate non-relativistic description of these systems.

Recent developments in drone technology have led to a proliferation of civilian and military unmanned aerial vehicles. This of course brings us closer to a reality depicted in films like Star Wars. Drones have become ubiquitous in various fields, including research, transportation, recreation, and package delivery. For the military, swarm drones offer the potential for surveillance, reconnaissance, propaganda, and combat purposes. In contrast to commercial applications, swarm drones used by military forces serve a different set of objectives. Distinguishing ourselves from existing research, our work shifts the focus from optimal control to a analytical perspective in this domain. Our approach involves analyzing existing literature on military drones and developing a novel framework for evaluating progress in this field using natural language processing. This is an interesting area of research where we can separate and distinguish various types of information found in academic papers. Our research is divided into two parts. First, we create a large dataset consisting of academic papers related to military drones and use it to train a Natural Language Processing model. This model enables the automatic categorization of papers into our established framework, consisting of subtopics such as surveillance, reconnaissance, propaganda, and combat. Secondly, we use the trained model to predict the subtopics of unseen papers. This could have practical applications in fields like automatic paper summarization and literature search. For example, researchers and developers can use our work to identify relevant studies in their area of interest and gain a better understanding of the objectives that have so far been overlooked. Furthermore, our search tool can be

Data from the timeeli project yielding 3D correlations of the Lyman-$\alpha$ flux at $z \sim 2 - 6$ provides substantial information about the distribution of neutral hydrogen within the universe. This information can be utilized to calculate $H$, the Hubble constant, as well as the primordial power spectrum and growth function across a range of redshifts utilizing a cosmological model. In the case of our analysis, we employed synthetic data to assess various analytical methods.
