Our findings suggest that incorporating higher degree angular correlations significantly enhances the accuracy of parameter estimation, particularly the Hubble constant. This is primarily due to the alignment of synthetic data power spectra and higher degree angular correlations being highly sensitive to the characteristics of the cosmological model. In the case of our analysis, we were able to estimate the Hubble constant, the baryon oscillation scale, and the growth factor with relative accuracies of 0.64%, 0.32%, and 4.35% based on analyzing just the $C(l)$ up to $l=20$ for ten separate simulations. These values decreased to 0.48%, 0.16%, and 2.48% when $C(l)$ up to $l=300$ was also utilized. One key limitation we identified is that none of the methods applied were capable of distinguishing the primordial power spectrum and model parameters such as dark matter density, neutrino mass, and spatial curvature.

Researchers at the Fermilab Accelerator have successfully demonstrated emittance transfer between transverse and longitudinal beams for the first time. The experiment utilized a specific $e^+e^-$ resonance decaying into light neutral mesons to study the temporal distribution of $e^-$ trajectories. The advanced beam manipulation and detection systems enabled precise measurement of the emittance transfer, which was then analyzed using simulated data to determine the actual value. The outcome agrees with the standard quantum electrodynamic model of emittance transfer.

Current studies on automatic driving and autonomous navigation have achieved significant progress in trajectory forecasting. Nonetheless, existing models typically generate potential future trajectories by extrapolating observed movements and overlook factors such as pedestrians' unpredictable nature and cars' cautious behavior. In our research, we introduce a novel model called SSCVAE, an innovative forecasting approach using a socially-aware, sequential approach. Leveraging socially-aware factors and a novel CVAE structure, SSCVAE produces a sliding forecast relevant to the subject's speed and accelleration, and also considers the surrounding environment. By integrating a novel efficient decoder with attention and an enhanced MOPO loss function, SSCVAE provides a more accurate forecast by measuring both the subject and the forecaster's discrepancy and their mutual information. Experimental evaluations using a heavily-annotated traffic dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model, revealing superior performance over state-of-the-art models in multi-step forecast accuracy and amino acidity content.

Research in computational complexity and deep learning has grown alongside the rise in high-performance computing capabilities. As high-resolution graphics and image processing capabilities advance, the underlying neural networks that facilitate these improvements become increasingly intricate. In an effort to grasp the nature of these sophisticated neural structures, researchers have turned to information theory. This theory provides a framework for assessing complexity using metrics such as entropy, mutual information, and redundancy. In particular, an experiment involving the application of Boltzmann machines to random graphs reveals that a key information-theoretic metric of complexity exhibits a sharp threshold. This finding has significant statistical consequences. Furthermore, the experiment demonstrates that optimizing a model's ability to approximate a target distribution using an information-theoretic metric of difficulty does not necessarily yield optimal results for other, potentially related systems. This phenomenon is referred to as a discrepancy in complexity and is rooted in the underlying system's inherent properties. This study is a preliminary exploration into the use of information-theoretic metrics of complexity in deep learning. It focuses on the underlying mathematical issues from a statistical perspective, encompassing topics such as inference, quantity measurement, correlation, and statistical data analysis. In addition to addressing these fundamental issues, the experiment raises significant statistical questions regarding the stability of optimization algorithms and the phenomenon of discrepancy in complexity. In response, this research provides statistical justifications for these phenomena.

This research presents a novel technique for hand gesture recognition using a compact convolutional neural network (CNN), designed to be employed on small embedded devices within unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems. Our approach focuses on developing a distributed human-UAV interaction system, allowing a single UAV to respond to multiple people in a group by capturing hand motion images and analyzing them using a tiny, high-performance hand gesture recognition CNN embedded on a computer module attached to the UAV. Our hand gesture recognition system is based on a compact end-to-end trained CNN, built on top of the VGG16 architecture with further optimized reductions. We tested the technique with a comprehensive dataset of 13 distinct hand gestures and achieved impressive results, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed method. This investigation also discusses how this technology can be applied to various autonomous aerial systems. Our study included an examination of the recognized gesture labels and explored the impact of the hand present in the images on the classification performance. With some enhancements, this technique could be adapted for more complex time-based hand gestures, enabling more in-depth analysis and allowing swarm behavior based on observed human activity.

The study aims to assess the feasibility of integrating deep learning approaches for classifying distinct blood cell types within an annotated blood image dataset. By combining various architectures of convolutional neural networks, we optimize our model, ultimately achieving an impressive categorization accuracy of 97.8% for five distinct blood cell types. This proposed method holds promise for expanding to other hematological classification tasks and may be adapted for other image analysis applications.

In various quantum engineering areas, there's a significant need to create quantum states efficiently, either as part of compiling quantum circuits or assembling the ground state in quantum simulators. Current methods for efficiently changing quantum states in closed systems or those in contact with an infinite-temperature environment face limitations. A distinct approach utilizes a counterdiabatic driving strategy that leverages a compatible Hamiltonian to dictate the target state and driving pace. Nevertheless, this method necessitates an adjustable Hamiltonian. We propose a variant of counterdiabatic driving that can change the ground state of a standard model, the Hubbard model. Using a compact effective Hamiltonian, we can achieve this change with any driving pace. The effectiveness of our approach, which is versatile and universal, is demonstrated. It's suitable for ground-state assembly in quantum magnets and various other models derived from the Hubbard model, such as the Heisenberg-X-Y model and lattice fermion models with double exchange, among others.

A new color space known as HUEtemp categorizes image colors into distinct temperature segments, spanning from warm hues (approximately 300K) to cool hues (above 600K), in addition to incorporating the inherent characteristics of an image's color palette. The proposed HUEtemp color space effectively captures these properties by combining each color's hue with its corresponding temperature, thereby enabling seamless differentiation between warm and cool regions within an image. The creation of this color space facilitates straightforward separation and recombination of image colors, thereby enabling various applications including high-velocity color changes, dcolored reflections, and simulation of material behaviors across warm-cool boundaries. This research presents an empirical approach for deriving the most plausible color temperature mapping rules across the entire warm-cool color spectrum.

This research investigates the behavior of a key parameter, $\alpha$, within the expanison about a fixed point as the variable $x$ approaches infinity in a complex plane, with specific considerations for functions displaying asymptotic behaviors in these regions. The primary focus lies in determining the properties and behavior of $\alpha$ in three primary categories of such functions, with one category defined by the behavior of a function as it approaches a specific type of singular point, another by the behavior of a function as a variable approaches infinity in a complex plane (essentially the inverse scenario to the first category), and a third defined by the behavior of a specific type of periodic functions. The most critical aspect of this research, however, revolves around establishing the concept of "exponential Taylor expansion" - a novel, fundamental discovery, which ultimately provides the groundwork for further exploration into the broader theoretical implications, notably the connection between singular asymptotic behaviors and Taylor expansions about fixed points as part of a deeper, unified mathematical framework.

Harmonic branched extensions are a significant component of harmonic analysis on manifolds. We establish the harmonic branched extension theorem for surfaces with a CAT($k$) metric, allowing for up to $2k+7$ branch points. Notably, this result complements the theorem of Alexander-Nagano for surfaces with positive curvature, and it also deviates from the traditional theory of harmonic functions on connected Riemannian surfaces. A novel proof technique employs geometric estimates and non-smooth Morrey's method. Additionally, this result has the potential to simplify the approach to the uniformization theorem for such surfaces.

A novel facility utilizing a high-power laser and magnetic wedge system has been developed to produce highly collimated, ultra-intense beams for scientific research. This facility combines state-of-the-art laser technology with a cutting-edge magnetic stage to create a state-of-the-art tool for scientific investigation. The integration of the magnetic stage allows for precise control over the laser beam's path, enabling (i) the generation of a nearly uniform plasma across the beam's diameter, (ii) the production of extremely narrow, tunable spectral lines through multiple-reflection plasma diagnostics, and (iii) the creation of intense, collimated beams with properties comparable to those generated by traditional methods, but with significantly enhanced low-energy sensitivity and spatial uniformity. The facility produces up to 100 kW of input power over a 30 cm diameter, with a 10% integration efficiency, along with a 50 kW/diameter output across multiple beam offsets, facilitating (i) the production of continuous monochromatic spectra through laser-plasma interaction, (ii) the separation of intense beams for high-energy applications, and (iii) the seamless transfer of laser energy between the source and target via a laser-plasma coupling process, enabling the production of intense beams in conjunction with a plasma wedge. The facility has been utilized in studies of nonlinear laser-plasma physics, including parametric mixing, frequency doubling, and continuum generation, along with a range of particle physics experiments, including beam collimation, off-axis focusing, and micron-scale target

In a simple extension of the Standard Model, specifically the 2-Higgs Doublet Model, where the potential is approached through different methods such as tree-level approach or including a theoretical correction in the $Z_2$-symmetric case, the model's behaviour is examined in relation to a theoretical constraint. We analysed how the tree-level approach affects the model's predictions for various observables by using a global fit in different scenarios, while also considering the impact of a theoretical correction on these predictions. Furthermore, we discussed the practical implications of this correction in terms of the model's validity and experimental limitations.

RDF data links data from different sources to create complex networks of interconnected information. However, this process often ignores the original data's structure, which can lead to inaccuracies and inefficiencies. To address this, we propose integrating Shape Expression (SHAPe) constraints into RDF and relational databases, allowing data to be directly transferred between these systems. By combining existing frameworks for RDF and SHAPe, we've developed a new approach to link data, which we've tested with actual data and constructs. This method enables a query on an RDF database to generate equivalent results on a relational database, subject to specific constraints specified through SHAPe.

A new field called statistical network economics has emerged, focused on the analysis of market prices and spreads, which are forms of discrete and bounded variables. To account for the inherent discreteness and boundedness, novel econometric methods have been developed, some of which rely on regression techniques that can handle such limitations. To provide an open-platform solution, a comprehensive R package called StoNED has been available since 2016. Building upon this foundation, a Python library called pyStoNED has been created, mimicking the original package's functionality while integrating it with popular machine learning and data analysis tools in Python. Specifically, pyStoNED includes three key components: market estimation using regression techniques that can handle bounded variables, boundary estimation where prices are bound, and visualization tools to display the results of these estimations. To showcase its effectiveness, pyStoNED is applied to daily yellow peeler market prices, demonstrating the ability to produce accurate market equations that incorporate price bounds, as well as related data such as spreads and skewness. Furthermore, the package allows users to seamlessly integrate data from external sources, such as the Quandl platform, which provides access to real-time market data. By offering a user-friendly platform for analyzing discrete and bounded market prices, pyStoNED facilitates market analysis and empowers users to explore price dynamics in greater detail.

In the standard model, the Higgs boson's weak coupling to top quarks makes it difficult to detect through its mixed production with top quarks and additional jets at the LHC. However, within certain extensions of the standard model, this coupling can be altered, allowing for new simulation studies at the LHC. This paper presents results for four distinct scenarios: a specific extension of the standard model, a specific expansion of the standard model, a specific expansion of the standard model with a specific relationship between particles, and an expansion of the standard model with hidden sectors. Using the LHC's data, these scenarios can be ruled out or supported within certain error margins under certain assumptions. Analysis of early LHC data supports the validity of these scenarios for certain error margins, while the paper also outlines potential improvements for detecting these scenarios in future analyses at the LHC.

Language models like BERT have proven highly effective at extracting insights from text, but their full potential is limited by the need for labor-intensive manual analysis to create relevant features. This research seeks to overcome this challenge by applying unsupervised and few-shot methods to enable more efficient and robust analysis. By utilizing various techniques such as data augmentation, generation of computational concepts, and program execution, we evaluate the performance of these approaches against established benchmarks and discover that a combination of these methods surpasses the effectiveness of traditional methods in many instances.

The accuracy of speech-to-text technologies has significantly improved in recent years, driven by advances in deep learning and the expansion of large, freely accessible data sets. Consequently, a variety of open-source German models has emerged for automated speech recognition, enabling diverse use cases across mobile devices, browsers, and embedded systems. Based on previous research, we examine the efficacy of deep learning-based German models and compare them to a high-performing English model. Our analysis focuses on two key performance indicators: the balance between accuracy and training time. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of a novel data augmentation approach, known as label noise, in improving model performance. Moreover, we evaluate the accuracy of different scale models across a range of data sizes.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear with theories involving both single and dual star evolutions, however through VLT telescopes, research in the Doradus star cluster has enabled a comparative analysis of spectral and radial velocity data. The results show 13 Be-type stars with precise rotation rates in the cluster, revealing a distinct separation between rapid rotators and slower ones. Additionally the research found 8 Be-type stars without companions that are in the process of shedding their outer layers, suggesting a distinct binary and solitary distribution within the cluster. The rotation characteristics of Doradus's Be-type stars are found to be similar to those of the SMC's Be-type stars, yet the rapid rotators in Doradus appear to be less abundant than in the SMC. The slower rotating Be-type stars in Doradus have rotation speeds closer to those of the cluster's slower rotating B-type stars, yet the rapid rotators show little similarity in their rotation speeds to the cluster's rapid rotating B-type stars. The data suggests that in the context of Doradus's high radial velocity dispersion, the binary model appears more suitable in explaining the origin of the Be-type stars. The minimum mass ratio needed for a binary evolution model to result in a Be-type star type is discussed. The research also found that in the cluster, Be-type stars are less abundant in number but beaming factors are more abundant compared to SMC's Be-type stars. The research discusses different predicted spectral types and binary probabilities

Several neural network approaches have been developed to remove noise from text datasets, crucial for analyzing and making data visualizations and insights feasible within reasonable computational limits. One such noisy text inversion technique revolves around improving the performance of Fully Conditional Continuous Neural Networks (FCCNNs), utilized in multiple applications, to descale and normalize datasets. This paper identifies two widespread text manufacturing methods as the primary sources of noisy data within FCCNNs and introduces an optimized data augmentation strategy to counteract these inconsistencies. The incorporation of data augmentation significantly enhances the predictive accuracy of FCCNNs by ensuring consistency in both vertical and horizontal dimensions during learning. The proposed method achieves an average improvement of 12% accuracy over existing techniques.

This paper demonstrates a variant of the Faber-Krahn conjecture for the first eigenvalue of the first Dirichlet eigenvalue for the Hermite operator when applying Robin boundary conditions, showing that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and derives the associated optimal mean curvature. Furthermore, under certain symmetry conditions, it is proven that this half-space remains the optimal configuration, which leads to the derivation of the Faber-Krahn inequality for the first Dirichlet eigenvalue.

NFT-K, a novel Bayesian non-parametric model, has been introduced by combining a network-based Dirichlet process (NBD) with a tangent space approach. Unlike traditional exchangeable models, NFT-K captures both inter- and intra-group variations and allows for distinct distributions across multiple clusters. By approximating NFT-K with tangent space techniques, we analyze its representability and develop an improved method for optimizing its kernel matrix. Furthermore, we derive a Bayesian approach for clustering and a procedure to make out-of-sample predictions that leverage NFT-K. Simulation studies and real-world applications demonstrate that NFT-K performs admirably in clustering mixed data, creating tasks, and understanding sequential content, while also surpassing state-of-the-art methods in accuracy.

In one-dimensional non-Hermitian systems, the non-Hermitian parameter $h$ can alter the periodic partitioning of the spectrum known as the non-Hermitian band gap, minimizing the number of gaps that occur. The architecture of the non-Hermitian band gap is subject to various conditions, such as driving the system non-periodic and introducing fluctuations in the parameter $h$. In our investigation, we explore a model describing one-dimensional Dirac fermions in the presence of random fluctuations in the $h$ parameter across distinct areas known as "ramps." As a result, the random fluctuations in $h$ lead to a shift in the system non-Hermitian band gap size from an optimal size in the disordered state to a minimal size at a specific critical transition point. Utilizing the multiscale perturbation method and the diffusion analysis, we explain both the system behavior in the ordered state and the critical characteristics of the two phases. Our research also reveals that the point-gap topology reduction can be observed under distinct conditions, such as when fluctuations in $h$ exceed a certain threshold in the disorder state. Additionally, we demonstrate a distinct reduction in correlations and the emergence of a boundary separating different types of localization as it pertains to the system's entire spectrum.

This study examines the impact of speech characteristics on listener perceptions, focusing on attributes such as friendliness, competence, and energy. We're interested in how these traits form opinions about the speaker and not just the content of the speech. We've identified two approaches to incorporate these characteristics into speech models. The first involves using a set of predefined attributes as a reference point. The second strategy conditions the speaker's voice on these attributes, allowing opinions to arise organically through the interaction between the listener and the speaker. We've created a set of friendly female voices using a text-to-speech system and conducted a listening test to understand how various speech characteristics affect the formation of opinions about the speaker. The results show that energy, specifically, has a significant impact on how friendly, competent, and energetic the speaker is perceived to be.

A type of modular $A_4$ symmetry is used in a model incorporating a $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge group, where the dark matter particles are assumed to be luminous, comprised of a $S_3$-generated $U(1)_{B-L}$ global symmetry. In this model, all standard model singlets and the right-handed Majorana fermions acquire masses through the effects of two distinct modular $A_4$ symmetries in a non-identical manner. This is achieved by incorporating two magical $S_4$ scions to form the modular group, one of which is used to create the standard model singlets, while the other is used to create the right-handed Majorana fermions. This model's particle spectrum is divided into three distinct groups based on their charges under the modular $A_4$ symmetry, $Z_3$, $Z_9$, and $Z_{12}$, which in turn allows for the creation of a dark matter network to investigate the effects of DM-LM transitions on the lunar neutrino flux. Furthermore, this model predicts a specific arrangement for the neutrino mass matrix, ultimately leading to the creation of four pairs of nearly degenerate light neutrinos, each with a very small mass, accompanied by a much larger $\Delta m^2_{LS}$ value, which in turn could be measured using lunar neutrino experiments.

In this research, the triaxial nuclear movement is examined, and the quadrupole collective motion is analyzed based on the Bohr-Mottelson model. We have extended this model to include the effects of the minimal length in quantum mechanics, and our findings indicate that the rotational bandwidth is adjusted in accordance with the minimal length, but its general shape remains unchanged. Additionally, our results show that the minimal length does not interfere with the characteristics of the collective movement.

This research proposes a new class of synthesized Golay complementary sets called creative Golay complementary sets, which are constructed from existing sets using a modulation method applied to their difference sequences. Specifically, we create these sets by modulating the difference sequences of various Golay sets (including the optimal Golay set) with distinct periodicity factors, before combining the modulation outcomes with specific complex values. To ensure the proposed sets maintain their complementary properties, we utilize a phase-shift keying (PSK) modulation method. Notably, we demonstrate the feasibility of generating creative GCSs with 13, 27, and 81 indices using this approach. Additionally, our study shows that creative GCSs can be configured to support multi-carrier systems, including 13- and 27-carriers, among others.

This paper explores a novel application of unsupervised alteration detection in hyperspectral images using a deep convolutional autoencoder. A straightforward training objective enabled parallel processing across 96 GPUs, significantly reducing training time. Employing a combination of encoder depths and a weighted loss function further improved the model's performance. Through extensive testing on diverse datasets, the top-performing model demonstrated high accuracy in detecting alterations and exhibited minimal sensitivity to changes in architecture parameters. Crucially, the model successfully identified alterations in sparse datasets, outperforming existing approaches. To facilitate reproducibility, a publicly accessible GitHub repository provides all necessary code and resources.

A rigorous approach has been developed for estimating the residual entropy of molecular fluids from their pair potential parameters. It's discovered that for a substantial class of pair potentials, including Lennard-Jones, the residual entropy is directly linked to the quasi-lattice configuration and can be calculated using a straightforward formula. Furthermore, the source of the contribution from a particular configuration is solely due to its kinetic energy, leading to a simple method for estimating the density-dependent residual entropy based on average energy differences between configurations and the host fluid. It's also found that a potential that mimics entropy can be derived from any pair potential, which compensates for the fluid's viscosity by reducing its density-dependent resistance to fluid flow. This effect is such that the potential's influence on viscosity is largely equivalent to the residual entropy's contribution. We discuss the scope and limitations of this method, particularly regarding its applicability to more complex molecular models involving multiple atom types and those with an evident structural pattern in their pair distribution functions.

We've developed a cosmological model that integrates the cyclic universe theory and the Lambda-CDM model by introducing an inflationary mechanism that addresses the cosmic evolution in three stages, reflecting the cyclic pattern. This pattern is not directly influencing the evolution process. By examining the deceleration parameter, cosmic expansion history, and the relationship between expansion and the Hubble parameter, our model's predictions align with observations of the Hubble-Lemaitre-Tolman models, resulting in a consistent cosmic evolution without a cosmic crisis. Our findings also indicate that the model's asymptotic behavior matches the Lambda-CDM model's characteristics. However, the model offers a new perspective on the Lambda-CDM model by reinterpreting certain aspects of our universe's evolution.

The Invariant-set hypothesis offers an interpretation of quantum correlations that could potentially be consistent with a hidden variables framework that doesn't involve nonlocality. We've developed a new model to test this idea, which we believe has the most comprehensive implementation of this hypothesis yet introduced. Our analysis suggests that achieving genuine quantum correlations likely requires values of invariant sets that extend beyond the typical range of continuity.

The proliferation of edge devices, including smart speakers, watches, and tablets, has led to a significant increase in data generated from IoT sources. In particular, applications such as speech-to-text and object detection have started adopting neural networks, which often require significant computational resources. A critical task in text-based apps is keyphrase detection, and this project investigates whether light neural network models can effectively handle this process on IoT devices. We examine two models, ReNet and SqueezeNet, comparing their performance in keyphrase detection tasks, and find that these models can successfully identify key phrases on IoT devices with limited capacity, such as the NVIDIA Jetson Nano. Notably, our key findings indicate that while these models may not achieve the superior performance of more complex neural networks, they are well-suited for integrating onto IoT devices due to their reduced parameter and memory requirements.

Using a discrete lattice approach, we examine the dimer coverage in a specific type of random walk on a non-orientable 2D lattice with an imposed gauge field. The dimer coverage corresponds to the mass ratio of the two fermion flavors in a concurrent lattice model of QCD. The interplay between the topology of the lattice and properties of the underlying gauge field, specifically flux, is investigated. It's shown that the dimer coverage at the lattice's boundary has a significant, non-trivial impact on the lattice as a whole, an property characteristic of 'lattice non-locality'. We establish that this effect can be transferred to a fermion system placed in a background gauge field. Additionally, using lattice models of QCD, we investigate the dimer coverage in regions defined by the lattice's inherent symmetry properties and find that the flux also exhibits a significant, non-trivial impact on the dimer coverage in these areas.

In the field of machine learning and signal processing, the group Lasso has been shown to efficiently select a single relevant category from a set of nominal features. However, this method's effectiveness is restricted when dealing with a large number of nominal categories, as it relies on the assumption that the features are compactly represented. To overcome this limitation, researchers developed an enhanced group Lasso approach that combines the potential category meanings into compact features. By doing so, they can be integrated into the standard group Lasso framework and solved using an efficient solver derived from the soft-thresholding technique. Moreover, our enhanced group Lasso has an added benefit of being able to select multiple relevant categories, not just one. To validate its performance, we conducted a series of experiments on data sets consisting of nominal variables, which consistently demonstrated that our enhanced method consistently produces better outcomes than traditional group Lasso. Our findings also indicate that the characteristics of the underlying data sets play a crucial role in determining the optimal number of features to select.

As the integration of virtualization grows in information and communication technology systems, including safety-critical ones, hypervisors need to be evaluated according to their performance in real-time systems. In this study, a v9MPSoC processor with Virtualization Assist technology is used as a multi-core platform for embedded real-time systems, and a custom-designed hypervisor, named T-Visor, is developed to meet the stringent requirements of real-time systems. To minimize the overhead of context switching associated with hypervisors, T-Visor incorporates a unique, lightweight design that integrates both paging and programing techniques for improved efficiency. A priority-based scheduling mechanism is also implemented to ensure real-time capabilities. Using the VxWorks-GR operating system as a benchmark, the authors compare the performance of this system when run natively and with the integration of T-Visor, and test it on various real-time scenarios. With the assistance of hardware virtualization technology, the context switching time of T-Visor remains below 1ms, and this value further decreases when using the 256KB and 512KB TLB. In addition, by introducing a Request/Response protocol to optimize data transmission between the Guest OS and Hypervisor, the authors achieve a communication time of less than 0.1ms. In real-time applications, such as the Traffic light control, the authors demonstrate how T-Visor efficiently manages multiple traffic light processes in an airport environment, and successfully implements a hardware-based trap

When capturing panoramic images with a mobile phone, unwanted elements often obstruct the view, necessitating the use of a panomorphous model to predict and fill in missing information. Instead of relying on the conventional minimum energy principle, this research explores an alternative solution by leveraging a gravitational potential model inspired by classical gravity theory. The simulations reveal that the minimal answer derived from this model is an optimal solution to the panomorphous model, and it also offers a useful direction for overcoming obstacles and tracking object movement in real-world applications. Our experimental results confirm the model's efficiency by demonstrating a notable 26% and 19% reduction in the total variation energy and the x-gradient energy, respectively, compared to the standard solution.

Our research explores the properties of a complex dynamic system, consisting of two interconnected groups, each containing an infinite number of identical elements, with the interaction between groups influenced randomly. We examine the possible behaviors of this system in response to different intensity levels of heterogeneity within the groups. Our analysis demonstrates that as heterogeneity within the groups becomes more evenly distributed, the system's dynamic response exhibits two possible patterns of oscillation: a pattern of synchronized, out-of-phase oscillation, or a pattern of partially synchronized, out-of-phase oscillation. Additionally, the system's stable mid-line path is found to display characteristics of a unique, attractively drawn path. We utilize advanced mathematical techniques to identify the boundaries that separate the system's different operational patterns and examine how these new findings impact the system's overall oscillatory behavior when compared to similar previous studies.

Controlling complex systems with uncertainties and limitations has become a significant challenge, despite recent advancements in learning-based controllers. The coherence of learned controllers is often compromised by these uncertainties and limitations, rendering them impractical for real-world applications. In complex systems, a single control failure can have catastrophic consequences, underscoring the need for controllers that can withstand failures. In this paper, a comprehensive approach is presented to develop robust and resilient controllers capable of withstanding control failures. The proposed method extends model-based policy search methods to address control reliability through probabilistic system reevaluation. By integrating probabilistic models into optimal control search, the controller learns to navigate through uncertainty and identify resilient control strategies. This approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear three-tailater system with limitations and uncertainties. The results show that the controller can effectively cope with control failures and limitations, while remaining close to optimal.

Building upon the concept of slice rings introduced by Bahriden and Gursel, we derive a natural algebraic structure on the hom-space between two slice rings, itself being a slice ring, by extending multi-layered diagrams. This enables us to form a two-spectrum consisting of the homogeneous slices of a unitary ring, and this structure has applications in k-theory through the derivation of a k-theory ring for spaces with finite CW-complexes based on their cellular decomposition.

By extending the concept of entanglement entropy to higher-order correlations, researchers have found an advantage in analyzing chaotic systems through tensor network methods. In this work, we introduce the refracted entropy, a correlation measure with higher order properties that we determine for chaotic systems using a fully hierarchical approach in tensor networks. By investigating the boundary-refracted entropy cross-sections, we discover that they follow the conformal Ward identity, an outcome consistent with earlier findings in chaotic systems. Moreover, our boundary-refracted entropy's central charge alignment with earlier results highlights the higher-order correlations' ability to withstand heat bath perturbations better than the entanglement entropy.

Living organisms rely on intricate patterns to maintain stability, attract preferences, and maintain coherence in their surroundings. These patterns often result from underlying processes and may be influenced by environmental conditions and genetic factors. Although environmental factors can lead to random fluctuations, the consistency of a pattern can still endure due to its genetic foundation. This concept underpins the diverse array of life on Earth, ranging from the complex patterns of the human brain to the symmetrical flowers of certain species. Our research focuses on this endurance, introducing the concept of heritability in patterns formed by spatially-related processes. We define a pattern's heritability as the combined effect of environmental and genetic contributions on its characteristics. Using the methods of stochastic processes and parameter representation, we explore the conditions that lead to pattern endurance. Our analysis applies to patterns formed by local transfer processes, such as heat or chemical reactions, and those defined by piecewise constant functions with uniform distribution within specific areas. We have identified the conditions under which piecewise constant patterns (characterized by constant values within separate regions) display pattern endurance. These conditions are related to the characteristics of the transfer processes and the layout of the pattern subregions. Our research provides a comprehensive approach for understanding pattern formation and endurance in various scientific and biological contexts.

The generalization of the three-dimensional H\'{e}non map was first presented by C. Carminati in 2008.  This generalized H\'{e}non map is defined by the iteration $ \vec{x}_{n+1} = (\phi(x_n, y_n), y_n, x_{n+1}) $ where $ \phi(x, y) = x + \alpha y f(x, y) $ and it's distinguished from the original H\'{e}non map by the inclusion of an extra variable and its effects on behavior.

The underlying principle of general relativity, Geometric Gravity, holds that test particles follow geodesic trajectories. This paper explores an alternative theory of gravity that deviates from Geometric Gravity by introducing a new concept - gravitational holonomy. The essence of Geometric Gravity lies in the non-integrability of the equations describing geodesic motion, resulting in the emergence of a new effect with properties analogous to the Zeeman or Strong-Cassini effects. The new gravity effect's effectiveness surpasses that of the Zeeman or Strong-Cassini effects, as it originates not only from the spin of the central body but also from its rotational state and the radial displacement of the test object. The scenario in which the central body is at rest reveals the gravitational holonomy effect reduces to the Zeeman effect.

Rivin and Rota previously found the number of nonnegative integer solutions to the equation $x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n = n-1$ where each $x_i$ is a multiple of $k$, and they developed a formula for counting such solutions in a specific set of positive integers. This formula uses the coefficients of the distribution of hook lengths in partitions, multiplied by $k$. These coefficients are found for $k=2$ and $k=3$ in this study. To obtain these coefficients, the study first identifies a set of partition hooks that are multiples of $k$, and then uses a two or three-fold approach, depending on $k$, to determine the distribution of these hooks. The main result for $k=2$ involves a generating function for even hooks in partitions, and the main result for $k=3$ involves a recursive relationship for counting three-multiples of partition hooks. Several secondary results were obtained in the course of the study.

Using the Larmor clock's method to measure a particle transitioning through a potential barrier, we find that certain asymmetries in the transition process can be linked to moments in time when energy changes occur due to its spin orientation and external magnetic influences. An external magnetic field impacts the particle by altering its energy by introducing an electric dipole moment, causing a delay in the particle's transition. For a particle passing through a barrier with an energy level below its rest energy, this delay, in turn, is proportional to the square of the external magnetic field strength. By adjusting the parameters such as energy and spin alignment, it's possible to observe tunneling effects directly using the Larmor clock method.

Dominant distribution patterns over P-wave mesons, defined by their orbital angular momentum states and coupling strengths to meson fields, vary significantly. Essentially, these patterns act as a mass-weighted version of the usual twist decomposition. In the context of QCD, dominant distributions, as opposed to the standard infinite twist decomposition, can better describe P-wave mesons, with higher-order distributions decreasing more rapidly with momentum. Notably, dominant distributions favor positive coupling strengths to meson fields, making them more suitable for practical use in constructing P-wave meson interpolating operators to study meson structure through lattice QCD.

We've developed a theoretical model for a "nonlinear switch," which can be achieved through a quantum system that induces a change in bosonic bath dynamics. Our study focuses on a "command" particle, represented by a two-level system, interacting with a Bose-Einstein condensate, modeled as a one-dimensional Tonks-Miura system. Our results show that the interaction between the two systems results in a sudden change in the dynamics of the condensate, effectively acting as a nonlinear switch, when the "command" particle undergoes a quantum transition. Our observations also indicate periodic periods of inactivity, determined by the strength of the interaction and number of "command" particles. Additionally, we analyzed how the presence of an external potential, resembling a soft-core well, influences the dynamics of the system, revealing an intriguing combination of coherent destruction of oscillations and periodic revival phenomena that is critically dependent on particle density.

Our mathematical framework based on the BMS algebra allows us to investigate the dynamics and symmetries of both classical and quantum theories involving numerous soft particles, where we define the challenge presented by extensive softness as a continuity rather than a issue of counting soft particles. This formulation helps us develop a new understanding of the concepts of subleading softness and charge conservation in systems with numerous soft particles. Our findings reveal that, in the context of the BMS algebra, the subleading soft current associated with any charge conservation law remains soft and conserves itself. This understanding also enables us to analyze the implications of the continuity character of softness on the properties of colors and charges in systems with numerous soft particles. Importantly, our research demonstrates that, while the counts of local symmetries become ambiguous, the continuous character of softness ensures the integrity of the BMS algebra and the conservation laws it upholds. This in turn facilitates the extension of our understanding to the quantum level, where we define a self-consistent version of the Bispectrum based on the BMS algebra.

In the rapidly evolving deep learning landscape, the typical approach to
classification involves utilizing a pre-trained neural network, either extracting
its feature mappings or making predictions directly and then fine-tuning. However,
when incorporating an online learning capability, most existing frameworks
experience performance degradation as training progresses due to a few
highly confident instances overpowering the ensemble. To address this concern,
we propose a novel Neural Structure for Online ensemble Learning capability,
whereby each training iteration, a dynamic instance is selected and incorporated
into an ever-changing learning ensemble. By designing the ensemble as a distinct
layer within the backbone network, we enable seamless end-to-end training without
requiring adjustments to the model architecture. Moreover, we devise an innovative
framework to automatically identify and exclude unreliable training instances,
whereby the selected training data are dynamically divided into separate training
sets for distinct learning pathways. As a result, our approach can consistently
maintain accurate classification while continuously learning from unstable classification
datasets. Experimental results on several datasets, including CIFAR, ImageNet,
and SunArt, demonstrate the substantial potential of this capability to enhance
general online learning outcomes.

The concept of generalized shapes in n-dimensional Euclidean space, defined by a measure with a certain property, has been expanded upon. In this expanded concept, a specific type of metric, known as Ricci-flat, is incorporated. It has been discovered that Euclidean space itself exemplifies a generalized shape with a particular type of measure. Furthermore, it was proven that any generalized shape in three-dimensional Euclidean space is the result of combining a Ricci-flat metric with a particular type of symmetry. Consequently, it was concluded that a generalized shape in four-dimensional Euclidean space encompasses a set of metrics characterized by constant scalar curvature.

Let $q$ be a power of $2$. We are working with $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ as our base field. Our study focuses on $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$-vector space permutations that are induced by fixed permutation functions with both domain and range in $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. By using linear functions, we establish a connection between these permutation functions and $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$-permutations, which allows us to count the number of these permutations. These counting results are extended to the scenario where the vector space has a dimension of $d \geq 2$. Our method also enables us to calculate the exact number of elements within certain degenerate sets of permutation functions. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions under which these permutation functions become complete permutation functions with respect to $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ as both their domain and range. Specifically, we identify and analyze universal conditions, necessary and sufficient conditions, and novel results concerning the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ representing these permutation functions, which also allows us to resolve a long-standing open problem originally posed by Tuza in a different context.

A computer-based technique for identifying intestinal worms relies on machine learning and image recognition algorithms. The goal is to develop an effective method for classifying worm species in stool samples, which will aid diagnosis and research in the field. A comprehensive database of worm species, "EWALD", has been utilized in this study to compare the accuracy of two machine learning models - Support Vector Machines and Deep Belief Networks - for image-based species categorization. The results indicate that a combination of unsupervised and supervised training in a two-stage Deep Belief Network process achieves higher accuracy and efficiency than the SVM method. Furthermore, DBN training utilizing data augmentation can attain excellent classification results even with a reduced number of classes, presenting valuable opportunities for future applications.

This research presents a novel estimation approach for a comprehensive class of
non-zero-sum investment and reinsurance strategies using a hybrid model combining
a finite state Markov chain and a diffusion process. We derive a specific
identification criterion for the model's parameters and offer a step-by-step
method for calculating them. A numerical optimization technique is employed to
solve for the strategies' variables. We also show the rate of convergence of the
estimation procedure under certain conditions. Furthermore, a simulation study
is conducted to evaluate the performance of the estimation method.

A proposed control approach in this research is designed to meet the demanding requirements of flight missions by utilizing a PIDA control strategy combined with genetic programming. To develop this method, the paper first explores neural network structure optimization using a stochastic dual simplex algorithm, then validates the resulting controller through rigorous testing within the Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Test Environment. The innovative PIDA control strategy is subsequently constructed, incorporating the optimized neural network structure and incorporating a genetic programming filter for enhanced performance. This control strategy is then tested in various challenging flight scenarios, demonstrating its reliability and effectiveness in executing complex missions.

This article outlines the central features of pion-nucleon interactions within the low-energy range, focusing on key implications for theoretical particle physics and nuclear physics. It provides an overview of how current experimental data suggest a significant deviation from the standard pion-nucleon interaction model as described by chiral effective theory, particularly with regard to the composite nature of pions. Additionally, the article notes a connection to the large scattering length of pions and nucleons, which is an essential characteristic at low energies and can be considered an inherent property.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment necessitates an in-depth reconstruction of the trajectories of charged particles created within high-energy particle collisions. For the realization of the CMS detector in 2009, a specific subset of recorded events, characterized by at least one charged particle within a proximity of less than 10 in from the impact point, was utilized for an initial assessment of the pixel detector's functionality. This analysis provides an independent evaluation of the pixel reconstruction algorithm using the so-called "hardware paths" as opposed to traditional reconstruction methods. The resulting trajectory resolutions were determined under conditions during the initial CMS data collection period with energies of 7 TeV during the 2010 and 2011 LHC runs. The investigation, referred to as CMS-PAS-EXO-12-035, involves an exclusive analysis of 7 TeV proton-proton collision data collected by the CMS detector. For the purpose of this analysis, a specific subset of events, characterized by at least one charged particle within a proximity of less than 10 in from the impact point, was utilized for an initial assessment of the pixel reconstruction algorithm. The precise trajectory resolution was determined to be approximately 3.4 in, in alignment with anticipated design standards. This study also confirms that the pixel reconstruction algorithm delivers accurate results for off-impact events. The analysis delves into and critically assesses each stage of the pixel reconstruction process using these events. The resulting findings, presented in the form of an so-called "

Our goal is to categorize the morphologies of 2,057 galaxy hosts with redshifts less than 1 from the HSC-ADR, which is an extensive and deep astronomical survey. We employ a machine learning-based system, combining two distinct neural networks, the first to predict a galaxy's overall shape and the second to refine its detail, utilizing features such as ellipticity and polarization to characterize complex structures. We develop and introduce three specific host galaxy classification categories to suit our model: simple, irregular, and distorted, each representing distinct morphological patterns. To ensure accuracy, our model is trained and tested using a database of 1,455 and 2,057 samples respectively, and is further validated through comparison with human assessments from the HSC-ADR, achieving high overall accuracy of 0.88 and specifically 0.85, 0.82, and 0.80 for the three categories mentioned above. The distributions of certain galaxy features also reveal notable disparities between the classifications, largely consistent with our expectations. The detailed results and specific definitions of each category are recorded in tables for future reference. The resulting dataset of classified galaxies can be utilized in future studies of the evolution of compact and distant galaxies.

Using a model based on the Varenne-Fontes-Ianni approach, researchers simulated and analyzed the structure functions of atomic nuclei as seen in electron scattering experiments. They investigated the impact of specific types of bonds within the nuclei, including those involving the sharing of space and momentum, and those characterized by the shifting of particles. Through the analysis, the team demonstrated the feasibility of distinguishing between these different types of bonds by looking at different regions of the resulting distribution.

This research enhances the functionality of complex-valued deep learning by applying complex number arithmetic across the network's co-domain, thereby considering the output's complex nature. The Deep Complex Networks technique, a widely-used approach for handling complex data with a single real channel, is found to be insufficient for achieving CDNN co-domain equality. This work presents a novel CDNN architecture with a new co-domain equality framework that can learn complex-weight matrices and bias vectors as complex values. The proposed method overcomes the limitations of the DCN approach and provides a comprehensive mathematical analysis of its performance. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the suggested CDNN framework in both basic component and feature learning applications.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the saturation of gluon distribution.  When gluon distribution becomes saturated, it establishes a distinct gluon density threshold per unit rapidity per rapidity,  Often referred to as the geometrical scaling condition, this threshold gives rise to noticeable scaling phenomena in various processes across a wide range of scales and energies.  In this chapter, the concept of saturation is first explained through theoretical formulations, and then, by comparing theoretical models to experimental findings, it demonstrates the presence of saturation and reveals the phenomenon of geometrical scaling that occurs across various processes.  Specifically, this chapter verifies the saturation of gluon distribution in ep scattering and proton-proton collisions at RHIC and the LHC, and in addition, it proves that geometrical scaling arises in parton-parton collisions, also known as minimum-bias and semi-inclusive processes.  Furthermore, it presents evidence of saturation that originates from a kinetic effect associated with gluon distribution in heavy nucleus collisions at the energies reached by the Gold and Lead nuclei at the RHIC.

A thorough examination of abundance spreads within the metal-poor globular clusters NGC 4147, NGC 4590, and NGC 5053 reveals the presence of multiple factors. While [α/Fe] ratios remain consistent, variations in [Fe/H], [Fe/Fe] (abundance spread), and [Fe/FM] (abundance dispersion from Fe to heavy elements) ratios consistently arise at the same [Fe/H] point. Specifically, abundance spreads among evolved stars are only present in the more metal-poor globular cluster, NGC 4147. Furthermore, the patterns of [α/Fe] ratios fall short of expected values, and the dispersion among the younger, young-rich clusters is significantly higher than that of older, metal-poor clusters. It's also found that the metal-poor globular clusters exhibit a higher FM abundance than α elements but with increased metallicity, the α elements surpass the FM abundance, contradicting the sustained α-suppression phenomenon. It's concluded that the FM stars and the abundance spreads among them originate from within the globular cluster itself, its PMS population, and may accurately represent the initial diverse composition of the metals within these clusters.

A recent machine learning forecast challenge aimed to predict academic performance across different fields, using a dataset from 13 US colleges and universities. Over 700 participants took part in the competition, submitting over 18,000 models and analyses. This paper makes three key contributions: Firstly, we develop an innovative, open-source toolkit incorporating established concepts from the influence function family to evaluate the performance of influence-based forecasts. Secondly, we provide a comprehensive assessment of the challenges in assessing influence-based forecasts, highlighting the need for distinct validation procedures. Finally, we compare the performance of the top-ranked models from the challenge and show that our influence-based approach can improve prediction quality, particularly in specific fields such as social sciences and education.

We introduce SQUID, a novel quantum technique for classroom learning that we've optimized for worst-case performance. This research advances quantum teaching methods, an emerging field that has previously been largely under-explored. We have compiled a comprehensive dataset of classification and clustering tasks, along with their corresponding difficulty levels, using a combination of manual and automatic assessment tools. This dataset will enable the evaluation of quantum teaching methods against established benchmarks. Furthermore, we have leveraged the state-of-the-art quantum computing capabilities of IBM devices to study the impact of different parameter settings on the performance of a cutting-edge quantum k-means algorithm in a real-world environment.

Researchers, specifically Meng, we study a specific type of submanifolds, namely distorted product pointwise semi-slant submanifolds, within nearly contact manifolds. A key point in our research involves establishing a critical constraint related to the Lee distribution, indicating that such submanifolds cannot exist when the Lee distribution is of rank greater than or equal to half the dimension of the ambient manifold. Additionally, we derive several criteria to determine the distinct characteristics of these submanifolds, including when they can be classified as Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian, and the specific forms of their metric and Levi-Civita connections. A key example is provided to illustrate the concepts presented in our study.

The PALEOCCENE project aims to develop an alternative method for detecting inactive, low-energy nuclear recoils utilizing optical properties of specific radiation damaged silicon nanocrystals. This effort considers post-production damage in silicon detectors to be a distinct, separate method from traditional irradiation-based detector development. The ultimate goal of PALEOCCENE is to design a prototype capable of distinguishing between elastic and inelastic nuclear recoil events at the low counting rate levels characteristic of dark matter experiments, specifically focusing on inelastic scattering. By achieving this, PALEOCCENE intends to take a significant step towards developing new-era, ultra-low-count rate portable devices for direct dark matter detection, as well as exploring fundamental physics at the nuclear level via inelastic scattering. Additionally, the research initiative recognizes the potential application of damaged nanocrystals in studying low-energy nuclear physics across a broad spectrum, including both isolated nuclei and projectiles at rest, thereby contributing to our understanding of the strong force via ab-initio quantum calculations.

The optimization of industrial processes and diverse biological systems in a state of constant change depends heavily on particles that are in constant motion. These particles draw upon energy from external sources, such as concentration gradients, to facilitate their movement. Our investigation focuses on how colloidal particles that are fixed in place but in constant motion respond within complex chemical environments through combined observations and theoretical modeling. When exposed to different concentrations of chemicals, the motion of the particles becomes influenced by the varying levels of this gradient, resulting in intricate patterns of movement. Our findings reveal a clear connection between the characteristics of the chemical mixture and the motion of the particles. Our research offers a new framework for the controlled movement of particles, potentially leading to the design of new materials and offering a fresh understanding of the complex movements exhibited by living systems.

This research examines the effects of a weak in-plane magnetic field on fractional quantum Hall effect in systems of two-dimensional electron gases confined by parabolic shapes. By using the density-matrix natural orbital representation and forming numerical models of up to 24 spin-orbit coupled Landau levels, it becomes possible to analyze total spectral densities with respect to both momentum and energy. Our findings show that applying a small magnetic field results in notable alterations in the resulting density distributions and magnetic susceptibilities. Additionally, we have identified and counted various hallmark structures within the density and spin-resolved spectral densities that we have dubbed "magnetorotons" - these features encompass both the underlying quadratic Landau levels and their combined spin-orbit counterparts. Our results demonstrate that the collective excitation patterns of the lowest energy states are predominantly strong-density features located at low energies and weak momentum. Moreover, we have found that the collective excitations in multiple observed magnetorotons undergo Luttinger liquid correlations as the in-plane magnetic field increases in strength.

Graph theory, mathematics and computer science offer various techniques for detecting outbreaks in systems, including disease transmission and neural activity, by identifying significant changes in activity across networks. This is achieved through the application of more complex algorithms than those used in traditional graph analysis. Many of these methods rely on adjusting parameters to balance the identification of various types of changes and have not been fully developed. This paper presents a simple, efficient technique for detecting outbreaks while preserving the underlying network structure. The approach involves reducing the likelihood of false positives by analyzing differences in activity and incorporating necessary details for understanding causes and effects. Additionally, this method incorporates clustering and relies on a new representation that preserves network features as geometric shapes.

To accurately estimate angular power spectra of Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) maps, a hybrid method combining maximum likelihood estimation and angular power spectrum estimation is proposed. This method aims to optimize the estimation of spectral parameters $a_{\ell m}$ in a model of CMB intensity, which incorporates cosmological parameters and instrumental noise across a range of multipole moments. The method leverages an approximate quadratic model of the likelihood function and uses an iterative algorithm to converge at optimal points. At these optimal points, instrumental noise effects are suppressed, much like in pseudo-$C(\ell)$ methods. In contrast to pseudo-$C(\ell)$ techniques, however, this method accounts for point-source cross-terms through a model-based instead of map-based approach, reducing contamination from X-factor residuals. In simulations using Planck 2018 intensity maps, cross-terms from three point sources were used to demonstrate the method's efficacy in reducing residual X-factor effects, particularly in the vicinity of point sources, without significantly distorting the primary CMB quadrupole and overall spectral shape. A comparative analysis with existing methods showed that this new approach yields CMB amplitude estimates similar to "masking" point sources, yet avoids the associated data loss, as well as achieving lower X-factor residuals than "joining" points sources into a few representative locations.

Autonomous agents can learn to achieve goals under specific restrictions by following instructions, which incorporates concept of object classes and their functions. However, successful implementation requires the ability to seamlessly identify objects that match these descriptions in response to changing circumstances. Current methods are crippled by object identification errors that occur as a result of discrepancies between the objects present in the environment and those referred to in the instructions. In this paper, we develop an innovative technique that overcomes reference inconsistencies by clearly defining object classes in terms of their characteristics. This technique employs a detection network that recognizes objects consistent with the descriptive attributes, thereby increasing its chances of success by focusing on objects that actually satisfy the given conditions. Our proposed approach excels in our proposed multi-room environment, comparing favorably with state-of-the-art techniques that rely solely on goal specifications. Additionally, we test its efficacy in a simulated cooking task, also making it available as an online game at http://multitask.cmu.edu/ldgol/.

Quantum shadow tomography is a widely used technique for estimating an unknown quantum state or channel. Yet, there's been limited research on channel shadow tomography compared to state shadow tomography, despite both being based on quantum measurement. In this research, we present an optimal protocol for channel shadow tomography, where our results reveal that the number of required measurements scales quadratically with the dimension of the channel and time, when using two distinct measurement settings. Interestingly, we confirm that channel shadow tomography requires more measurements than state shadow tomography. Additionally, we validate the practical applicability of our results by applying them to specific channels, namely, the depolarizing channel and quantum channels associated with random waves functions.

Keen's inequalities for a range of shapes in the plane have been established. For a given shape, defining the Minkowski sum as the combination of two shapes when one is dilated by a certain scale factor, known as the Keen parameter, these inequalities state that a certain ratio remains bounded within a specific interval. Specifically, for a dilated shape S_d, a particular ratio equals or exceeds 1 plus the Keen parameter times a specific value, and this value or excess repeats in reverse for the original shape S. Certain values for this ratio have been established for basic shapes. Furthermore, it was shown that there exists a shape, called the super-equal square, with a ratio equal to 2, thereby providing an answer to a long-standing question. These inequalities have been established for a variety of shape types in the plane. Additionally, a similar set of inequalities has been proven for shapes in the plane that involve a certain area and a certain width, a concept proven previously by Lagarias.

This study investigates the application of drones in time-sensitive operations, utilizing them as relay stations to maintain a stable connection while in motion. The device can host multiple applications such as satellite communication, internet services, and data transmission via the cloud. A specific use case involves drones acting as satellite relays for areas with limited or no direct satellite signal access. To address this, a path-planning algorithm is developed to minimize drone flight time while maintaining a connection with the fixed ground station and ensuring coverage of the service area via the drone's mounted antenna. A comprehensive mathematical model is presented, including its formulation and sub-programs to tackle the optimization problem. The resulting approach is tested and evaluated through simulation of different scenarios.

In our theoretical study of thermal fluctuations' impact on bilayer graphene at room temperature, we employed the Renormalization Group method to derive an effective Hamiltonian. Our analysis shows that Coulomb interactions between distinct layers lead to an instability of the initial state, resulting in order developing in one layer while the other exhibits fluctuations. This instability is a result of anisotropic metric adjustments and is analogous to the Kardar-Bratisyuk mechanism. We found the effective low-energy Hamiltonian for the ordered layer to be equivalent to the repulsive 1/2 fractional quantum Hall state's Hamiltonian, specifically the composite fermons form. We used the RG method to demonstrate that the coupled motion of two layers is unstable, with this occurrence equivalent to the appearance of a non-trivial fixed point. We investigated the physical consequences of this non-trivial fixed point and found that the composite fermions form near the Van Hove singularities of the dispersion relationship's extrema. We also established a correspondence between this phenomenon and the observed spontaneous symmetry breaking in the charge density wave state of the repulsive 1/2 fractional quantum Hall system. Our calculations show that the correlation length and the associated temperature-driven renormalization of interlayer coupling are linked to the coupling strength as follows: $\xi \propto (\lambda^{-1})^{1/2}$, with the exponent depending solely on the filling factor $e.g. 1/2$. This phenomenon bears resemblance to the Berezinskii

The conformation of surface molecules significantly affects their functions, particularly in responses to temperature variations. Studying the thermal effects on molecular shape is crucial, especially for molecules with distinct forms, such as the Pr-Center-containing (PC) molecule Sc2TbN@C80, which exists in multiple conformations. In this research, the PC molecule's conformations were examined on an h-BN/Ni(111) substrate at temperatures ranging from 90 K to room temperature by using STM imaging. The experimental results showed that, at low temperatures, the PC molecule favors a 2:1 (Sc:Tb) ratio and adopts a quasi-cubic (QC) shape, which transforms into a plane-augmented hexagonal (PAH) shape with a 1:2 (Sc:Tb) ratio as the temperature increases. The distinct shapes of these molecules were identified through STM imaging and confirmed by DFT calculations. Furthermore, the simulations demonstrated that the QC and PAH configurations have comparable stabilities, which corresponds to the coexistence of these structures at intermediate temperatures. The current findings illustrate the thermal-induced change in molecular conformation and establish a basis for investigating the correlations between molecular structure and property in low-dimensional systems, including temperature-dependent configurations.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes human-made and natural objects, equipped with unique identifiers, to facilitate identification and efficient data exchange. As the majority of these devices are in danger due to the lack of modern security measures, which are typically too resource-intensive for them, we recommend an efficient technique. The proposed approach is centered around a novel light seal algorithm, which is based on the original work by Zhong et al. but has been optimized for deployment on low-energy devices. The modified light seal algorithm showcases superior performance when compared to the advanced encryption standard, verifiable homomorphic encryption, and password-based authenticated key exchange versions 2 in terms of computational efficiency, memory requirements, and energy consumption. Additionally, we have tested the time it takes to perform both the light seal algorithm and its original counterpart as well as the new random oracle version. The results confirm the original and new random oracle versions of the light seal algorithm exhibit non-adaptive and weak non-adaptive security, which is equivalent to the original work, at 96 and 95 byte sizes, respectively.

Accurate time measurement via GPS receivers is crucial in various applications, but their performance can be compromised due to environmental interference and the inherent limitations of time-stepping schemes. A notable example of this is the GPS receiver's inability to sample certain moments, a challenge that can be overcome by simulating a continuous sampling process using the Bayesian theory of sequential measurement. Our research explores the application of this theory to accommodate the inherent shortcomings of current measurement techniques. By adopting a sequential Bayesian approach, we can derive an adaptive algorithm that refines and updates the measurement process based on real-time feedback, ultimately achieving the optimal performance that would be attained in a continuous sampling process. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that this algorithm's performance can be calculated analytically, enabling the prediction of its results even before its execution, and allowing for a stopping criterion to be established based on the attainment of a desired performance level. A model-based test case confirms that this algorithm can effectively adapt to distinct scenarios, such as variations in signal strength and signal types, and even in situations where the received signals are subject to a periodically changing frequency shift. Additionally, our method has been found to be suitable for implementing on embedded systems with limited resources.

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive theories, focusing primarily on nearest neighbor graph geometry and message spreading dynamics. Despite their importance, existing methods fail to capture the multi-scale structure of networks and are often influenced by specific scales. To address this limitation, a new theory termed Gromov theory is introduced, which measures the scale-free properties of geometric networks using a metric called Gromov centrality. By analyzing networks at varying scales, Gromov centrality surpasses traditional centrality methods, enabling the detection of multi-scale patterns and patterns influenced by network triangles. Furthermore, a polynomial algorithm is developed to calculate Gromov centrality, with experimental results demonstrating its capabilities in multi-scale network analysis.

The Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravity is presented as an expansion of Newton's theory of gravity. It's capable of explaining phenomena that are inaccessible to Newton's law, including their higher-degree analogs. Its mathematical structure mirrors that of the Yukawa potential in certain aspects. This theoretical framework is also discussed in the context of modern cosmology, including the formation of structures within it. We're presenting a comprehensive derivation of the bi-spherical Yukawa potential, which was previously described in passing. In addition, two distinct methods for calculating the mass of a sphere in this theoretical framework are outlined and validated against established measurements. We're exploring the properties of dark matter using the theory, which reveals that the dark matter density is consistent throughout the universe and is unaffected by local variations in curvature. In this theoretical framework, the total energy of the universe is determined by the sum of its intrinsic, kinetic, and gravitational energies, which is found to be finite. This theoretical model also addresses the fundamental question of how the universe came to be in a state of uniform expansion. In this theoretical framework, gravitational force varies inversely with the square of the mass of the objects involved, which facilitates the observation of discrete properties such as spin angular momentum. This theoretical model is normally referred to as the "Gravity II" theory.

This study centers on various intrinsic properties of matrix pencil families, which can be viewed as subsets of matrices of a specific rank. The paper's key contributions include conceptual advancements, accompanied by comprehensive definitions and theoretical proofs that utilize practical examples to illustrate the results. These outcomes have significant implications for the development of algorithms in control theory, particularly in the field of infinite spectrum identification.

Building on  \cite{deCanio21}, we broaden the application of  $T^*T$-duality to a broader class of examples.  The strategy employed in \cite{deCanio21} involved utilising a combination of  $T^*$-duality and  ${\mathbb Z}_N$-duality.  We successfully remove the restriction to  ${\mathbb Z}_N$-bundles, replacing it with a more general condition involving  ${\mathbb Z}^{(k)}$-bundles for $k \geq 1$, where the definition of the latter will be recalled in this current paper.  We also enhance the existing method by introducing a novel  $T^*T$-duality geometric criterion, which is permanently included within the paper.

We show that any planar graph $G$ with $\Omega((\mathfrak{c}^2/w(G)) \cdot \log |M|)$ vertices can be embedded into a proper $K(w(G), G)$-metric with $\mathfrak{c}$-approximation ratio. In the special case where $w(G) = 2$, this implies that planar graphs with treewidth $<8$ can be embedded into a 2-approximation metric. Additionally, we show that for any $k$-free graph $G$ with treewidth $<\mathfrak{c}$, $k$-partite graphs with treewidth $<2\mathfrak{c}$, or chordal graphs with treewidth $<2\mathfrak{c}$, a $k$-approximation metric can be embedded into a proper $K(k, G)$-metric with $\mathfrak{c}$-approximation ratio.

For smooth, strongly monotonic discrete-time dynamical systems, considering random initial conditions and noise in the right variable as perturbations, we analyze the long-term behavior of random trajectories.
